q: Why did Transformers replace RNNs?
a: Three reasons. Parallelism: an RNN must process token t before token t+1, while self-attention processes all tokens of a sequence at once, so training uses GPUs far better. Path length: in an RNN information between distant tokens passes through many steps and fades (vanishing gradients); in attention any two tokens interact directly in one step. Scaling: because training is parallel and stable, Transformers could be scaled to billions of parameters and trillions of tokens, and quality kept improving with scale. The cost is attention's \(O(n^2)\) time and memory in sequence length, which motivated FlashAttention, sparse attention and state-space models.

q: Why does deep learning dominate images and text, while gradient boosting still wins on tabular data?
a: Images, audio and text are raw, high-dimensional signals with local structure (pixels near each other, words in order). Deep networks learn hierarchical features from them, which beats anything hand-designed. Tabular data is already featurized: columns are meaningful, heterogeneous (prices, categories, counts), often small, and have irregular, axis-aligned decision boundaries. Tree ensembles handle mixed types, missing values and monotonic thresholds natively, need little tuning, and are robust to uninformative features. Neural nets on tabular data tend to need much more tuning and data to match them. Many production systems therefore use GBDTs for tabular signals and neural networks for embeddings of text or images, sometimes feeding one into the other.

q: What changed between GPT-3 and ChatGPT?
a: Mostly post-training, not architecture. GPT-3 was a base model trained to continue internet text, so a question might be answered, ignored, or continued with more questions. InstructGPT and ChatGPT added supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstrations, then RLHF: a reward model trained on human preference comparisons, and PPO to optimize the model against it with a KL penalty to stay close to the SFT model. The result follows instructions, holds a conversation, refuses some harmful requests, and was preferred by people even at much smaller sizes (a 1.3B InstructGPT model was preferred over 175B GPT-3 in the paper's evaluations).

q: Why did diffusion models overtake GANs for image generation?
a: GANs produce sharp images but train as an adversarial game, which is unstable and prone to mode collapse (covering only part of the data distribution). Diffusion models train with a simple, stable regression loss (predict the noise that was added), cover the distribution well, and are easy to condition on text through cross-attention and classifier-free guidance. Their weakness, slow sampling over many denoising steps, was reduced by better samplers, latent-space diffusion (Stable Diffusion), distillation and flow matching.

q: What is the difference between a language model, an assistant and an agent?
a: A language model predicts the next token; a base model just continues text. An assistant is a language model post-trained (SFT plus preference tuning) to follow instructions and converse safely. An agent is an assistant placed in a loop with tools: it decides which action to take, observes the result, and continues until a goal is met. What makes it an agent is that the model chooses the control flow, rather than a fixed sequence of calls written by a developer (which is a workflow).

q: What is self-supervised learning, and why was it the key to LLMs?
a: Self-supervised learning creates labels from the data itself, for example "predict the next word" or "fill in the masked word". It needs no human annotation, so the training set can be the whole internet. Next-token prediction at that scale forces a model to learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and code, which then transfer to downstream tasks with little or no labeled data. The same idea powers contrastive image models such as CLIP and masked autoencoders in vision.

q: Where does knowledge live in pretraining, fine-tuning and <abbr title="Retrieval-Augmented Generation">RAG</abbr>?
a: Pretraining stores broad knowledge in the weights; it is expensive and frozen at a cutoff date. Fine-tuning adjusts the weights, which is good for behavior, format, style and domain language, but unreliable and costly for teaching many new facts. RAG keeps knowledge outside the model in a searchable store and inserts relevant passages at query time, so it is fresh, private, citable and access-controlled, but limited by retrieval quality. Production systems often combine them: a fine-tuned model for behavior plus RAG for facts.

q: Where does classical ML still beat LLMs in production?
a: On structured prediction at scale with tight latency and cost budgets: fraud scoring, credit risk, demand forecasting, ad click prediction, ranking. Gradient-boosted trees or logistic regression run in microseconds, are cheap, calibrated, explainable, and easy to monitor and retrain. LLMs are better for unstructured inputs (text, documents, conversation) and open-ended generation. A strong answer mentions combining them: for example LLM-generated features or embeddings feeding a GBDT, or a classical model routing requests before an LLM is called.

q: Tell me about a model you shipped. How did you choose the metric?
a: Structure: business goal → what a mistake costs (false positive vs false negative) → offline metric that reflects that cost → online metric that measures the business goal → guardrail metrics. Example shape: "For fraud, a missed fraud cost about 40 times a false alarm, so we optimized recall at a fixed false-positive rate of 1% offline, measured PR-AUC across thresholds, and tracked prevented losses and manual-review volume online." Then mention how you checked the metric moved together with the business outcome.

q: How do you approach an ML problem you've never seen before?
a: Clarify the goal and how success is measured; check whether ML is needed at all (rules or heuristics can be the baseline); look at the data (size, labels, leakage risks, time structure); build the simplest baseline end to end; choose an offline metric aligned with the business cost; iterate on data and features before model complexity; validate properly (time-based splits where relevant); plan the online test and monitoring. Interviewers want to hear "baseline first" and "measure before adding complexity".

q: Your model performs well offline but poorly in production. What do you check?
a: In order: training–serving skew (features computed differently online, missing values filled differently, stale features); data leakage in offline evaluation (future information, duplicates across splits, target leakage); distribution shift (population, seasonality, a new product flow); label definition or delay (online labels differ from training labels); feedback loops (the model changes the data it later trains on); and the metric mismatch (the offline metric doesn't track the business outcome). Compare feature distributions offline vs online, replay production traffic through the offline pipeline, and check the experiment setup itself (sample ratio mismatch).

q: How would you explain a complex model's decision to a non-technical stakeholder?
a: Start from the decision and its business impact, not the algorithm. Use global explanations (which factors matter most overall, from SHAP or permutation importance) and local ones (why this specific case got this score) in plain language, with examples. Be explicit about uncertainty and limits: correlation is not causation, and importance is not the same as "changing this will change the outcome". Offer guardrails: human review for borderline cases, monitoring, and an appeal path.

q: What does a dot product measure, and why use cosine similarity for embeddings?
a: The dot product \(a \cdot b = \|a\|\|b\|\cos\theta\) grows with both alignment and length. Cosine similarity divides out the lengths, so it compares only direction. For embeddings, direction carries meaning while length often reflects frequency or confidence, so cosine is more robust. If all vectors are normalized to unit length, dot product and cosine give identical rankings, which is why many vector stores normalize once and then use the faster dot product.

q: Explain <abbr title="Singular Value Decomposition">SVD</abbr> and give two ML uses.
a: Any matrix factors as \(X = U\Sigma V^\top\): orthogonal input directions \(V\), scaling by singular values \(\Sigma\), orthogonal output directions \(U\). Truncating to the top \(k\) singular values gives the best rank-\(k\) approximation. Uses: PCA (principal components are the right singular vectors of the centered data matrix), recommender systems (low-rank factorization of the user–item matrix), compression of weight matrices, latent semantic analysis, and the low-rank view behind LoRA.

q: Derive the <abbr title="Mean Squared Error">MSE</abbr> loss from maximum likelihood.
a: Assume targets are the model output plus Gaussian noise: \(y = f(x) + \epsilon\), \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\). The log-likelihood of one point is \(-\frac{(y - f(x))^2}{2\sigma^2}\) plus a constant. Summing over data and maximizing is equivalent to minimizing \(\sum (y_i - f(x_i))^2\). So MSE is the right loss when errors are roughly Gaussian; heavy-tailed errors call for MAE or Huber loss instead.

q: How is a prior related to regularization?
a: MAP estimation maximizes log-likelihood plus \(\log p(\theta)\). A zero-mean Gaussian prior gives \(\log p(\theta) = -\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2\) + const, which is L2 regularization. A Laplace prior gives \(-\lambda\|\theta\|_1\), which is L1. The regularization strength \(\lambda\) corresponds to how tight the prior is: a stronger prior belief that weights are small means more regularization.

q: A disease affects 1% of people; a test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific. You test positive. What's the chance you're sick?
a: About 50%. Per 10,000 people: 100 are sick and 99 test positive; 9,900 are healthy and 99 of them falsely test positive. So 99 of 198 positives are real. The point interviewers want: when the base rate is low, even an accurate test yields many false positives. The same applies to fraud and rare-event detection, which is why precision matters so much there.

q: What is a p-value? What are type I and type II errors?
a: A p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as yours assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true. A type I error is rejecting a true null (a false positive), controlled by the significance level α. A type II error is failing to reject a false null (a false negative); power is \(1 - \beta\). Lowering α reduces false positives but increases false negatives unless you collect more data.

q: What does the Central Limit Theorem say, and why does it matter in ML?
a: The mean of many independent, identically distributed samples is approximately normally distributed, with variance \(\sigma^2/n\), whatever the original distribution (given finite variance). It justifies confidence intervals and z/t-tests on averages and conversion rates in A/B tests, and explains why mini-batch gradients are noisy estimates whose noise shrinks as batch size grows.

q: Why is the gradient of softmax plus cross-entropy so simple?
a: With logits \(z\), probabilities \(p = \text{softmax}(z)\) and one-hot label \(y\), the loss is \(L = -\sum_k y_k \log p_k\). Differentiating through the softmax, the terms cancel to \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = p - y\): predicted minus true. It's well-behaved (no saturation when the model is confidently wrong), which is one reason cross-entropy trains classifiers better than MSE on probabilities. Logistic regression's gradient \((p - y)x\) is the two-class case.

q: Why don't we use Newton's method to train neural networks?
a: Newton's method needs the Hessian, a \(d \times d\) matrix of second derivatives. For a model with \(d = 10^9\) parameters that's \(10^{18}\) entries to store, and inverting it costs \(O(d^3)\). It also behaves badly on non-convex losses, where it can move toward saddle points. Instead we use first-order methods with cheap curvature approximations, such as Adam's per-parameter scaling.

q: Why cross-entropy instead of <abbr title="Mean Squared Error">MSE</abbr> for classification?
a: Three reasons. It is the maximum-likelihood loss for categorical labels, so it's statistically correct. Its gradient with softmax or sigmoid is \(p - y\), which stays large when the model is confidently wrong, while MSE through a sigmoid has a gradient scaled by \(\sigma'(z)\) that vanishes in saturated regions. And combined with sigmoid it is convex in the logistic regression weights, while MSE through a sigmoid is not.

q: Forward vs reverse <abbr title="Kullback–Leibler divergence">KL</abbr> divergence: which is mode-seeking?
a: Reverse KL, \(D_{KL}(q\|p)\), is mode-seeking: \(q\) is heavily penalized for placing mass where \(p\) is near zero, so it locks onto one mode. Forward KL, \(D_{KL}(p\|q)\), is mode-covering: \(q\) is penalized for missing any region where \(p\) has mass, so it spreads out. Maximum likelihood training minimizes forward KL from data to model; variational inference typically minimizes reverse KL.

q: What is perplexity?
a: The exponential of the average per-token cross-entropy: \(\text{PPL} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_t \log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\right)\). It can be read as the number of equally likely choices the model is effectively choosing between at each step. A perplexity of 10 means the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice over 10 tokens. It's only comparable between models with the same tokenizer and test set.

q: Eigenvalues of a covariance matrix: what do they tell you?
a: Each eigenvalue is the variance of the data along its eigenvector. Large eigenvalues mark directions where the data spreads out; tiny ones mark nearly redundant directions. Their ratio to the total shows the share of variance each principal component explains, which is how you choose how many components to keep in PCA. A near-zero eigenvalue also signals multicollinearity, which makes linear regression unstable.

q: Explain the bias–variance trade-off with an example.
a: Bias is error from a model being too simple for the pattern; variance is error from being too sensitive to the particular training sample. Example: fitting house prices with a straight line (high bias, it misses the curve) versus a degree-15 polynomial (low training error, but it swings wildly between points, high variance). Increasing complexity lowers bias and raises variance, so validation error is U-shaped. You diagnose by comparing training and validation error, and you trade them off with model size, regularization, more data and ensembling.

q: How do you detect and fix overfitting?
a: Detect it with a large gap between training and validation performance, or validation loss rising while training loss keeps falling. Fixes: more or augmented data; regularization (L1/L2, dropout, weight decay); a simpler model or fewer features; early stopping; ensembling such as bagging; cross-validation for model selection so you don't overfit the validation set itself.

q: Does adding more data reduce bias or variance?
a: Mainly variance. More data makes it harder for a flexible model to fit noise, so the training–validation gap shrinks. It does little for bias: if a linear model can't represent a curved relationship, more data won't fix that. Learning curves tell you which case you're in.

q: L1 vs L2 regularization: why does L1 produce sparse weights?
a: Geometrically, the L1 constraint region is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes; loss contours usually first touch it at a corner, where some weights are exactly zero. L2's region is a circle, so it shrinks weights without zeroing them. Analytically, L1's penalty gradient has constant size \(\lambda\) regardless of the weight's magnitude, so it can push small weights all the way to zero, while L2's gradient \(2\lambda w\) vanishes as \(w\) shrinks. Use L1 for feature selection and L2 for stability with correlated features; Elastic Net combines both.

q: What is data leakage? Give three examples.
a: Information unavailable at prediction time that reaches training or evaluation. Examples: (1) fitting a scaler or target encoder on the full dataset before splitting; (2) a random train/test split on time-ordered data, so the model trains on the future; (3) a feature that is a consequence of the label, like "chargeback filed" in a fraud model; (4) the same user appearing in both train and test. Symptoms: suspiciously high offline metrics and a big drop in production. Prevent with time-based or grouped splits, pipelines that fit preprocessing inside folds, and asking of each feature whether it exists at prediction time.

q: How do you cross-validate a time-series model?
a: Never shuffle. Use forward-chaining splits: train on periods 1..k and validate on period k+1, then expand (or roll) the window and repeat. Leave a gap between train and validation if features use look-back windows or labels arrive late. Compute features point-in-time so nothing from the future leaks in. Report the average and the spread across folds, and check performance on the most recent fold, since that's closest to production.

q: Why is random search often better than grid search?
a: Usually only a few hyperparameters matter much. With a 3×3 grid over two hyperparameters you test only three distinct values of each; nine random points test nine distinct values of each. So for the same budget, random search explores the important dimensions more finely. Bayesian optimization goes further by using past results to choose the next trial.

q: Which models need feature scaling, and which don't?
a: Models based on distances or gradient-based optimization with penalties need scaling: kNN, k-means, SVM (especially RBF), PCA, linear and logistic regression with regularization, and neural networks (for stable training). Tree-based models (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting) don't, because a split only depends on the ordering of values within a feature.

q: How do you encode a categorical feature with 10,000 values?
a: One-hot is too wide and sparse for most models. Options: target encoding (replace each category by the smoothed mean of the target, computed out-of-fold to avoid leakage); frequency encoding; the hashing trick into a fixed number of buckets; learned embeddings in a neural model; or native categorical handling in CatBoost or LightGBM. Group rare categories into "other". Mention leakage and smoothing for target encoding; that's what interviewers listen for.

q: How do you handle missing data?
a: First ask why it's missing: completely at random, related to other features, or related to the value itself (for example, high earners skipping an income question). Options: drop rows or columns if missingness is rare or a column is mostly empty; impute with median or mode; model-based imputation (kNN, iterative); add an is_missing flag because missingness can carry signal; or use models that handle missing values natively, such as XGBoost. Always fit the imputer on training data only.

q: Explain the curse of dimensionality.
a: As the number of dimensions grows, the volume of the space grows exponentially, so a fixed amount of data becomes sparse. Distances concentrate: the ratio between the nearest and farthest neighbor distances approaches 1, so "nearest" stops meaning much. kNN, k-means and kernel methods degrade, and you need far more data to cover the space. Remedies: feature selection, dimensionality reduction (PCA, autoencoders), regularization, or models that learn compact representations.

q: Your fraud dataset is 0.5% positive. How do you build a model?
a: Use PR-AUC and recall at a fixed false-positive rate (set by review capacity) rather than accuracy. Split by time and group by customer to avoid leakage. Start with a GBDT using class weights or scale_pos_weight; try undersampling the majority within the training fold only. Tune the threshold to the business cost of a missed fraud versus a false alarm. Recalibrate probabilities if you resampled. Add anomaly-detection signals for new fraud patterns, and monitor drift, since fraudsters adapt.

q: Class weights vs resampling: when would you use each?
a: Class weights change the loss without changing the data: no information is thrown away and nothing is duplicated, and most libraries support them. Undersampling speeds up training on huge datasets but discards majority data. Oversampling or SMOTE can help models that can't take weights, but risks overfitting duplicated or synthetic points. Both distort predicted probabilities, so recalibrate. In practice: class weights first, undersampling when data is huge, and always threshold tuning.

q: Generative vs discriminative models: give examples and trade-offs.
a: Discriminative models learn \(P(y \mid x)\) or the boundary directly: logistic regression, SVM, most neural classifiers. Generative models learn how the data is produced, \(P(x \mid y)P(y)\) or \(P(x)\): Naive Bayes, GMMs, HMMs, VAEs, GPT, diffusion. Discriminative models usually give better accuracy with enough data. Generative models can work with less data (Naive Bayes on tiny text sets), handle missing features, detect outliers by low likelihood, and generate new samples.

q: What is the i.i.d. assumption and when does it break?
a: That training and test examples are drawn independently from the same distribution. It breaks with time (seasonality, trends, drift), groups (many rows per user, so rows aren't independent), feedback loops (the model influences future data, as in recommendations), selection bias (you only observe labels for approved loans), and adversaries (fraudsters adapt). When it breaks, random splits overestimate performance, so use time-based or grouped splits and monitor drift.

q: What is double descent?
a: As model capacity grows, test error first follows the classical U-curve, peaks near the interpolation threshold (where the model can just fit the training data exactly), then decreases again as capacity keeps growing. It has been observed with model size, training time and data size. It helps explain why very large neural networks generalize well despite being able to memorize: among the many solutions that fit the data, gradient descent tends to find smooth, low-norm ones.

q: Precision vs recall: give a case where each matters more.
a: Recall matters when missing a positive is expensive: cancer screening, fraud before a large transfer, safety-critical defects. Precision matters when false alarms are expensive or erode trust: spam filtering (losing a real email), auto-blocking accounts, notifications. Most real systems set a constraint on one and optimize the other, for example maximize recall subject to precision ≥ 90%, or maximize recall at the number of cases a review team can handle per day.

q: What does ROC-<abbr title="Area Under the Curve">AUC</abbr> mean intuitively? When is it misleading?
a: It's the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, so it measures ranking quality across all thresholds. It's misleading under heavy class imbalance: with 1,000,000 negatives, 10,000 false positives is only a 1% false-positive rate, so ROC looks great while precision is poor. It also ignores calibration and the operating point you'll actually use. Use PR-AUC or precision/recall at the chosen threshold for rare positives.

q: ROC-<abbr title="Area Under the Curve">AUC</abbr> or PR-<abbr title="Area Under the Curve">AUC</abbr> for fraud detection, and why?
a: PR-AUC (average precision), plus recall at a fixed false-positive rate or at the review team's capacity. Fraud is rare, so ROC's false-positive rate is diluted by the huge number of legitimate transactions, while precision directly shows how many flagged cases are real. The PR baseline equals the fraud rate, which makes improvements easy to interpret. Report both if stakeholders are used to ROC-AUC, but decide with PR-based metrics.

q: Why is F1 a harmonic mean rather than an arithmetic mean?
a: The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so F1 is only high when both precision and recall are high. With precision 1.0 and recall 0.02, the arithmetic mean is 0.51 but F1 is about 0.04, which better reflects a useless model. If the two errors have different costs, use Fβ or a cost-weighted metric instead.

q: Macro vs micro averaging: when does each matter?
a: Macro-averaging computes the metric per class and averages, so every class counts equally; use it when rare classes matter (rare diseases, minority intents). Micro-averaging pools all decisions, so frequent classes dominate; for single-label multiclass it equals accuracy. Report macro when you care about performance on every class, micro when you care about overall throughput, and per-class numbers when stakeholders care about specific classes.

q: What is calibration and how do you fix a miscalibrated model?
a: A model is calibrated if, among cases where it predicts 0.8, about 80% are positive. Check with a reliability diagram, expected calibration error or Brier score. Fix it on a held-out calibration set with Platt scaling (logistic regression on scores), isotonic regression (monotonic, needs more data), or temperature scaling for neural networks (divide logits by a learned \(T\), which keeps rankings unchanged). Recalibrate after resampling, after reweighting, and periodically under drift.

q: When do calibrated probabilities matter more than ranking?
a: When the probability feeds a decision with costs or money: ad bidding (bid = value × predicted click probability), insurance pricing, credit limits, expected-value triage, combining several models' outputs, or showing confidence to users. If you only ever take the top-k, ranking metrics are enough; as soon as the number itself is used, calibration matters.

q: <abbr title="Mean Absolute Error">MAE</abbr> vs <abbr title="Root Mean Squared Error">RMSE</abbr>: when do you use each?
a: RMSE squares errors, so it punishes large errors much more; use it when big misses are disproportionately costly, and note that it's sensitive to outliers. MAE treats errors linearly and is robust to outliers. The best constant predictor is the mean under MSE and the median under MAE, which tells you what each metric pushes a model toward. Report both when error distributions are skewed.

q: How can R² be negative?
a: \(R^2 = 1 - SS_{res}/SS_{tot}\) compares the model with always predicting the mean of the target. On a held-out set, a model that does worse than that constant has \(SS_{res} > SS_{tot}\), so R² goes below zero. It signals a badly overfit model, a distribution shift, or a broken pipeline.

q: Explain <abbr title="Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain">NDCG</abbr>.
a: It scores a ranked list with graded relevance, discounting relevance by position: \(\text{DCG@}k = \sum_i rel_i / \log_2(i+1)\), then divides by the DCG of the ideal ordering so scores lie between 0 and 1 and are comparable across queries. It rewards putting the most relevant items first, handles multiple relevance levels, and is the standard offline metric for search and recommendation ranking. Mention the variant with gain \(2^{rel}-1\).

q: <abbr title="Mean Reciprocal Rank">MRR</abbr> vs MAP vs <abbr title="Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain">NDCG</abbr>: which would you use when?
a: MRR when only the first relevant result matters (question answering, navigational search). MAP when there are several relevant items with binary relevance and you care about all of them. NDCG when relevance is graded (perfect, good, fair) and position matters. For RAG retrievers, recall@k is often the first metric to check, because the generator can only use what was retrieved.

q: How do you decide the sample size and duration of an A/B test?
a: From the baseline rate (or variance), the minimum detectable effect worth acting on, the significance level (usually 5%) and power (usually 80%): roughly \(n \approx 16\,p(1-p)/\delta^2\) per group for conversion metrics. Divide by daily eligible traffic to get the duration, then round up to whole weeks to cover weekly cycles. Smaller effects need quadratically more users; variance reduction like CUPED reduces it.

q: What is peeking, and why is it a problem?
a: Checking results repeatedly and stopping as soon as p < 0.05. Each look is another chance for noise to cross the threshold, so the real false-positive rate ends up far above 5%. Fix the sample size and duration in advance, or use methods built for continuous monitoring (sequential tests, always-valid p-values), and decide stopping rules before the test.

q: What is sample ratio mismatch?
a: When the observed split between groups differs significantly from the designed split, for example 50.6% vs 49.4% with millions of users. It means randomization, eligibility or logging is broken (bots filtered in one arm, a crash in the treatment, a redirect dropping users), so the result can't be trusted. Check it with a chi-square test before reading any metric.

q: Your offline metric improved but the online metric dropped. Why might that happen?
a: The offline metric may not reflect the goal (higher AUC on clicks, but fewer purchases). Offline evaluation may be biased by logged data from the old model (position bias) or by leakage. Features may differ in production (training–serving skew). The new model may be slower, and latency costs engagement. Users may react to change itself (novelty). Or the test is underpowered or broken (SRM). Investigate segment by segment and replay production data offline.

q: A/B test vs multi-armed bandit: when do you use each?
a: A/B tests give clean causal estimates with confidence intervals; use them for launch decisions and when you need to understand effects, including on guardrails. Bandits shift traffic toward better variants during the experiment, reducing the cost of showing a bad variant; use them for short-lived choices with many options (headlines, creatives, recommendations) where maximizing reward during the test matters more than precise inference.

q: What's interleaving and why is it efficient for ranking?
a: You merge the results of two rankers into one list (for example team-draft interleaving) shown to the same user, then credit each ranker for the clicks its items receive. Because each user compares both rankers directly, between-user variance disappears, so interleaving detects ranking differences with far fewer users than an A/B test. It measures preference between rankers, not absolute business metrics, so teams typically interleave to screen candidates and A/B test the winner.

q: Derive the normal equation for linear regression.
a: The loss is \(\|Xw - y\|^2 = (Xw - y)^\top(Xw - y)\). Its gradient is \(2X^\top(Xw - y)\). Setting it to zero gives \(X^\top X w = X^\top y\), so \(w^* = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) when \(X^\top X\) is invertible. Mention the cost (\(O(d^3)\) for the inverse), that singularity comes from collinear features or \(d > n\), and that ridge adds \(\lambda I\) to make it always invertible.

q: What are the assumptions of linear regression?
a: Linearity of the relationship; independent errors; constant error variance (homoscedasticity); approximately normal errors (needed only for inference such as p-values and confidence intervals, not for unbiased point estimates); and no perfect multicollinearity. Say how you'd check each: residual-vs-fitted plots for linearity and heteroscedasticity, autocorrelation tests for independence, Q–Q plots for normality, VIF for multicollinearity.

q: Why use squared error for linear regression?
a: It's the maximum-likelihood loss if the noise is Gaussian, it gives a convex problem with a closed-form solution, and its gradient is simple. Its weakness is sensitivity to outliers, because errors are squared; use MAE or Huber loss when errors are heavy-tailed.

q: What is multicollinearity, and how do you detect and handle it?
a: Strong correlation among features, so one is nearly a linear combination of others. Predictions can still be fine, but coefficients become unstable (large variance, possible sign flips) and hard to interpret. Detect it with a correlation matrix or the variance inflation factor, \(\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)\) where \(R_j^2\) comes from regressing feature \(j\) on the rest; values above 5–10 are a warning. Handle it by dropping or combining features, PCA, or ridge regularization.

q: R² vs adjusted R².
a: R² is the share of variance explained relative to predicting the mean; it never decreases when you add features, even useless ones. Adjusted R² penalizes the number of features: \(1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-d-1}\), so it only rises if a new feature improves fit more than chance would. For predictive models, prefer held-out error or cross-validation.

q: Why can't you use linear regression for classification?
a: It outputs unbounded values that aren't probabilities, the squared-error loss on 0/1 labels is pulled around by points far from the boundary (a correctly classified extreme point still generates large error and moves the line), and it isn't the right likelihood for binary outcomes. Logistic regression fixes all three with the sigmoid and log loss.

q: Why don't we train logistic regression with <abbr title="Mean Squared Error">MSE</abbr>?
a: MSE through a sigmoid is non-convex in the weights, so optimization can get stuck, and its gradient includes the factor \(\sigma'(z)\), which vanishes when the model is confidently wrong, so learning stalls exactly where it should be strongest. Log loss is convex for logistic regression and its gradient \((p - y)x\) stays large for confident mistakes. It's also the correct maximum-likelihood loss for Bernoulli labels.

q: Derive the gradient of the log loss.
a: With \(p = \sigma(z)\), \(z = w^\top x\), and \(L = -[y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)]\): \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial p} = -\frac{y}{p} + \frac{1-y}{1-p}\), and \(\frac{\partial p}{\partial z} = p(1-p)\). Multiplying gives \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = p - y\), and so \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = (p - y)x\). Averaged over data: \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top(p - y)\).

q: How do you interpret a logistic regression coefficient of 0.7?
a: A one-unit increase in that feature, holding others fixed, increases the log-odds by 0.7, which multiplies the odds by \(e^{0.7} \approx 2.01\). It does not double the probability: going from odds 1:1 (p = 0.5) to 2:1 gives p ≈ 0.67, but from 1:99 (p = 0.01) to 2:99 gives p ≈ 0.02. The effect on probability depends on the starting point.

q: Is logistic regression a linear model?
a: Yes, in the sense that matters: the log-odds are a linear function of the features, and the decision boundary \(w^\top x + b = 0\) is a hyperplane. The output probability is a non-linear (sigmoid) function of the score, but that doesn't make the boundary curved. Non-linear boundaries need engineered features, kernels, or a different model.

q: What happens to logistic regression on perfectly separable data?
a: The likelihood keeps increasing as the weights grow, because making the sigmoid steeper pushes predicted probabilities closer to 0 and 1. The weights diverge toward infinity and the optimizer never converges. L2 regularization (or early stopping) keeps the solution finite and well-defined.

q: Softmax regression vs one-vs-rest.
a: Softmax trains all classes jointly with one cross-entropy loss, producing probabilities that sum to 1 and comparable scores across classes. One-vs-rest trains \(K\) independent binary classifiers; it's simple and parallel, but scores aren't calibrated against each other and probabilities don't sum to 1. Use softmax for mutually exclusive classes; use independent sigmoids for multi-label problems where several labels can be true.

q: Ridge vs lasso: when would you use each?
a: Ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients smoothly, has a closed form, handles correlated features by spreading weight across them, and is a good default when most features carry some signal. Lasso (L1) sets some coefficients exactly to zero, which selects features and gives sparse, interpretable models, but it picks arbitrarily among correlated features. Elastic Net combines them. Scale features first and tune \(\lambda\) by cross-validation.

q: Why is logistic regression still used in production for click-through prediction?
a: It trains and serves extremely fast on billions of sparse, hashed features; its probabilities are well calibrated, which matters because bids multiply predicted click probability by value; it's easy to update online, debug and explain; and with engineered feature crosses it's surprisingly competitive. Deep CTR models (Wide & Deep, DCN, DeepFM) add learned interactions, often keeping a logistic "wide" component.

q: How does an <abbr title="Large Language Model">LLM</abbr>'s output layer relate to logistic regression?
a: The final layer maps the last hidden state \(h\) (dimension \(d\)) to logits over the vocabulary with a matrix \(W\) of shape \((V, d)\), applies softmax, and is trained with cross-entropy against the next token. That's multinomial logistic regression with \(V\) classes on top of features learned by the Transformer. The gradient with respect to the logits is again \(p - y\).

q: How does k affect bias and variance in kNN?
a: With \(k = 1\), the prediction follows every training point, including noise: zero training error, very high variance, a jagged boundary. As \(k\) grows, predictions average over more neighbors, which smooths the boundary and lowers variance but raises bias; at \(k = n\) every prediction is the majority class. Choose \(k\) by cross-validation; prefer odd \(k\) for binary problems and distance weighting when neighbors vary in distance.

q: Why does kNN struggle in high dimensions?
a: Distances concentrate: as dimensions grow, the nearest and farthest neighbors become almost equally far, so "nearest" carries little information. Data also becomes sparse, so the neighbors of a point aren't really close. And irrelevant features add noise to every distance. Mitigations: feature selection, dimensionality reduction, learned embeddings where distance is meaningful, and approximate indexes for speed.

q: How would you make kNN fast over 100 million vectors?
a: Use an approximate nearest-neighbor index: HNSW (a layered proximity graph with high recall at low latency, but memory-heavy), IVF (cluster vectors, search only the closest clusters), and product quantization to compress vectors so they fit in memory. Libraries such as FAISS, ScaNN, or a vector database implement these. You trade a little recall for orders-of-magnitude speed-ups; tune recall vs latency on a held-out query set.

q: Why is Naive Bayes called naive, and why does it still work?
a: It assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, which is almost never true (words co-occur). Its probabilities are therefore badly calibrated, but classification only needs the correct class to have the highest score, and that ordering is often preserved. It also has very few parameters, so it learns well from tiny datasets.

q: What is Laplace smoothing and why is it needed?
a: If a word never appeared with a class in training, its estimated probability is zero, and because Naive Bayes multiplies probabilities, one unseen word zeroes the entire class score. Laplace smoothing adds a pseudo-count \(\alpha\) (often 1) to every count: \(\frac{\text{count} + \alpha}{\text{total} + \alpha|V|}\). Smaller \(\alpha\) (Lidstone smoothing) is often better for large vocabularies.

q: Naive Bayes vs logistic regression: when does each win?
a: Naive Bayes is generative and makes strong assumptions, so it reaches its (lower) best accuracy with very few examples. Logistic regression is discriminative and makes weaker assumptions, so with more data it usually wins and gives better-calibrated probabilities. Choose Naive Bayes for tiny datasets, very fast baselines or streaming updates; logistic regression otherwise.

q: What are support vectors?
a: The training points that lie on the margin boundaries or violate them (inside the margin or misclassified). They're the only points with non-zero Lagrange multipliers, so the decision boundary is a combination of them alone. Removing any other point doesn't change the model. Few support vectors means a sparse model and fast prediction.

q: Explain the kernel trick in plain words.
a: Many algorithms, including SVMs, only use data through dot products between points. A kernel is a function that returns the dot product the points would have after mapping them into a richer feature space, without computing that mapping. So you get a linear classifier in a high- or even infinite-dimensional space (RBF kernel) at the cost of evaluating a simple function on pairs of points. The catch: you need the \(n \times n\) kernel matrix, which doesn't scale to very large \(n\).

q: What do C and γ do in an RBF <abbr title="Support Vector Machine">SVM</abbr>?
a: C sets how much margin violations cost: large C fits the training data tightly (narrow margin, overfitting risk), small C allows violations for a wider, smoother margin. γ sets the reach of each training point: large γ makes the RBF very narrow, so the boundary bends around individual points (overfitting); small γ makes it broad and smooth (underfitting). They interact, so tune them together on a logarithmic grid.

q: Hinge loss vs log loss.
a: Hinge loss \(\max(0, 1 - y f(x))\) is zero once a point is correctly classified beyond the margin, so well-classified points stop influencing the model; that produces sparse solutions (support vectors) but no probabilities. Log loss never reaches zero, so every point keeps a small influence, and it yields calibrated probabilities. Both are convex upper bounds on the 0–1 loss.

q: Why don't SVMs scale to very large datasets?
a: Kernel SVM training solves a quadratic program whose cost grows roughly quadratically to cubically with the number of samples, and the kernel matrix needs \(O(n^2)\) memory: 1 million points means \(10^{12}\) entries. Prediction cost also grows with the number of support vectors. Linear SVMs trained with SGD (or libraries like LIBLINEAR) do scale, and kernel approximations (random Fourier features, Nyström) help, but at that size deep networks or boosted trees are usually better.

q: When would you still choose an <abbr title="Support Vector Machine">SVM</abbr> today?
a: Small to medium datasets with many features where you want a strong, robust baseline: text classification with TF-IDF features (linear SVM), bioinformatics, some signal-processing tasks, or as a classifier on top of fixed embeddings. Also when you need a convex problem with a well-understood optimum. For large tabular data use boosted trees; for raw images, audio and text use pretrained neural networks.

q: Gini impurity vs entropy: what's the difference, and does it matter?
a: Both measure how mixed the classes in a node are and are maximal when classes are evenly split. Gini is \(1 - \sum p_k^2\); entropy is \(-\sum p_k\log p_k\). They choose the same split in the vast majority of cases. Gini is slightly faster (no logarithm) and is scikit-learn's default; entropy is a bit more sensitive to changes in small class probabilities. In practice it rarely matters; depth and minimum leaf size matter far more.

q: How does a tree choose a split on a continuous feature?
a: It sorts the feature's values and evaluates candidate thresholds between consecutive distinct values (or bin boundaries in histogram methods), computing the impurity reduction for each, and keeps the best across all features. Sorting costs \(O(n \log n)\) per feature, but sorted orders can be reused, and histogram binning reduces it to roughly \(O(\text{bins})\) per feature.

q: Why do decision trees overfit, and how do you prevent it?
a: A tree can keep splitting until each leaf holds one sample, memorizing noise: low bias, very high variance. Prevent it with depth limits, minimum samples per leaf or split, minimum impurity decrease, cost-complexity pruning, or by averaging many trees (random forest) or using shallow trees in boosting.

q: Why don't tree models need feature scaling?
a: A split only asks whether a value is above or below a threshold, so any monotonic transformation of a feature (scaling, log) leaves the ordering of values, and therefore the possible splits, unchanged. Distance- and gradient-based models need scaling; trees don't.

q: Bagging vs boosting.
a: Bagging trains models independently on bootstrap samples and averages them; it reduces variance, works best with deep, low-bias trees, and is parallel (random forest). Boosting trains models sequentially, each correcting the errors of the ensemble so far; it reduces bias, uses shallow weak learners, and is sequential (AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGBoost). Boosting is usually more accurate when tuned; bagging is more robust and harder to overfit.

q: Why does a random forest sample features at each split?
a: Averaging reduces variance only to the extent the trees are uncorrelated: \(\operatorname{Var} = \rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B\). Without feature sampling, every tree would split on the same strong features near the top and look alike. Sampling about \(\sqrt{d}\) features per split forces trees to use different features, lowering \(\rho\) and making the average much better.

q: What is out-of-bag error?
a: Each tree's bootstrap sample omits about 37% of the rows (\(e^{-1}\)). For each row, predict using only the trees that didn't train on it, and compute the error over all rows. It's an almost unbiased estimate of test error without a separate validation set, useful for tuning random forests cheaply.

q: Does adding more trees overfit a random forest? What about boosting?
a: Adding trees to a random forest doesn't overfit; error decreases and then plateaus, because each tree is an independent average term. In boosting, adding trees keeps reducing training loss, so after some point validation error rises: boosting can overfit with too many trees, especially with a high learning rate. Use early stopping on a validation set.

q: Explain gradient boosting as gradient descent in function space.
a: Treat the vector of predictions \(F(x_i)\) as the parameters. The gradient of the loss with respect to each prediction tells you how to change it to reduce the loss. A new tree is fit to the negative gradients (pseudo-residuals), which approximates a gradient step that generalizes to new points, and is added with a small learning rate. For squared error the pseudo-residuals are the ordinary residuals; for log loss they're \(y - p\).

q: Why use shallow trees in boosting but deep trees in random forests?
a: Boosting reduces bias by adding many small corrections; each learner should be weak (high bias, low variance) so the sequence doesn't overfit quickly, and depth controls the interaction order captured per tree. Random forests reduce variance by averaging; each tree should be strong and low-bias (deep), because averaging can't fix bias but does cancel variance.

q: What makes XGBoost better than vanilla gradient boosting?
a: A second-order (gradient and Hessian) approximation that gives closed-form optimal leaf weights and a principled split gain; explicit regularization on leaf count (\(\gamma\)) and leaf weights (\(\lambda\), \(\alpha\)); sparsity-aware split finding that learns where missing values go; row and column subsampling; and systems work (parallel split finding, weighted quantile sketch, cache-aware blocks, out-of-core training) that makes it fast on large data.

q: Write the optimal leaf weight and split gain in XGBoost.
a: With \(G\) and \(H\) the sums of gradients and Hessians in a leaf, the optimal weight is \(w^* = -G/(H + \lambda)\), and the leaf's contribution to the objective is \(-\frac12 G^2/(H + \lambda)\). A split's gain is \(\frac12\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda} - \frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}\right] - \gamma\). The split is made only if the gain is positive, so \(\gamma\) acts as a minimum-gain pruning threshold.

q: LightGBM leaf-wise growth vs level-wise growth.
a: Level-wise growth (XGBoost's default) expands all nodes at one depth before going deeper: balanced trees, more conservative. Leaf-wise growth (LightGBM) always expands the single leaf with the largest loss reduction: lower loss for the same number of leaves and faster convergence, but deeper, unbalanced trees that can overfit small datasets. Control it with num_leaves, max_depth and min_data_in_leaf.

q: How do XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values?
a: During split finding they try sending all missing values left and then right, and keep the direction with the higher gain. That "default direction" is stored per split and used at prediction time. Missingness can therefore be informative without imputation. CatBoost treats missing values as a separate value by default.

q: How does CatBoost handle categorical features without leakage?
a: Plain target encoding uses each row's own label to compute its category's average, which leaks the target. CatBoost uses ordered target statistics: it shuffles the rows and encodes each row's category using only the target values of rows earlier in that order (with a prior for smoothing), and uses several permutations. Combined with ordered boosting, this removes the prediction shift that causes overfitting.

q: Why is impurity-based feature importance misleading?
a: Mean decrease in impurity is computed on training data and favors features with many possible split points (continuous or high-cardinality features, even random IDs), and it splits credit arbitrarily between correlated features. Use permutation importance on validation data (shuffle one feature and measure the performance drop) or SHAP values, and remember that importance is not causality.

q: When would you choose a <abbr title="Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees">GBDT</abbr> over a neural network?
a: For tabular, structured data of small to medium size with heterogeneous features, when you need strong accuracy with modest tuning, fast CPU inference, native handling of missing values, and good explainability (TreeSHAP). Choose neural networks for raw text, images and audio, very large datasets with high-cardinality IDs that benefit from learned embeddings, multimodal inputs, or when you need to train end to end with other neural components.

q: What is stacking, and how do you avoid leakage when stacking?
a: Stacking trains a meta-model on the predictions of several base models. To avoid leakage, the meta-model's training features must be out-of-fold predictions: for each fold, base models are trained on the other folds and predict this one, so no base model predicts a row it trained on. At test time, base models retrained on all data (or the average of fold models) produce the meta-features.

q: Explain the k-means algorithm and its objective.
a: k-means minimizes the within-cluster sum of squared distances to centroids. Initialize \(k\) centroids (k-means++), assign each point to its nearest centroid, recompute each centroid as the mean of its points, and repeat until assignments stop changing. Each step lowers the objective, so it converges, but to a local optimum, so run multiple initializations. Cost is \(O(nkd)\) per iteration.

q: How do you choose k in k-means?
a: Look for an elbow in the within-cluster sum of squares as \(k\) increases; maximize the average silhouette score; use the gap statistic (compare with a reference uniform distribution); or use BIC with a GMM. Most importantly, check stability across random seeds and whether the segments are useful and actionable for the business decision. There's often no single "true" \(k\).

q: Why k-means++ initialization?
a: Random initialization can place several centroids in one cluster and none in another, giving poor local optima and slow convergence. k-means++ picks the first centroid at random and each next one with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest chosen centroid, spreading them out. It comes with an \(O(\log k)\) approximation guarantee in expectation and usually converges faster to better solutions.

q: When does k-means fail?
a: With non-spherical shapes (rings, elongated clusters), clusters of very different sizes or densities, outliers (they drag centroids), unscaled features (large-scale features dominate the distance), categorical data (means don't make sense; use k-modes), and high dimensions where distances concentrate. Alternatives: GMMs for elliptical clusters, DBSCAN or HDBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise, spectral clustering for graph-like structure.

q: Explain the EM algorithm.
a: EM fits models with hidden variables by alternating two steps. The E-step computes the posterior over the hidden variables given current parameters (for a GMM, each point's responsibility for each component). The M-step re-estimates parameters to maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood under those posteriors (responsibility-weighted means, covariances and weights). Each iteration never decreases the likelihood, but EM can converge to a local optimum, so initialize carefully (often with k-means).

q: <abbr title="Gaussian Mixture Model">GMM</abbr> vs k-means.
a: Both need \(K\). k-means makes hard assignments and assumes spherical, equal-variance clusters; it's faster. A GMM makes soft probabilistic assignments, learns a covariance per component (elliptical clusters of different sizes and orientations), gives a density model you can use for likelihoods and anomaly scores, and supports model selection with BIC. k-means is a special case of a GMM.

q: DBSCAN vs k-means: when would you use each?
a: Use k-means for large data with roughly round, similar-sized clusters when you know or can choose \(k\). Use DBSCAN when clusters have irregular shapes, you don't know how many there are, and you need outliers labeled as noise (geospatial points, anomaly-rich data). DBSCAN struggles with clusters of different densities (use HDBSCAN) and in high dimensions, and requires choosing ε and minPts.

q: What do ε and minPts mean in DBSCAN, and how do you choose them?
a: ε is the neighborhood radius; minPts is the minimum number of points within ε for a point to be a core point. A common heuristic sets minPts to about twice the number of dimensions, then plots each point's distance to its minPts-th nearest neighbor in sorted order and picks ε at the knee of that curve. Too small an ε labels most points as noise; too large merges clusters.

q: Derive <abbr title="Principal Component Analysis">PCA</abbr> as variance maximization.
a: Project centered data onto a unit vector \(u\): the variance of the projection is \(u^\top S u\), where \(S\) is the covariance matrix. Maximize it subject to \(u^\top u = 1\) with a Lagrange multiplier: \(S u = \lambda u\). So \(u\) must be an eigenvector of \(S\), and the variance equals its eigenvalue \(\lambda\); the best direction is the top eigenvector. Each next component is the top eigenvector orthogonal to the previous ones.

q: How are <abbr title="Principal Component Analysis">PCA</abbr> and <abbr title="Singular Value Decomposition">SVD</abbr> related?
a: For centered data \(X = U\Sigma V^\top\), the covariance is \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top X = V\frac{\Sigma^2}{n}V^\top\). So the right singular vectors \(V\) are the principal components, the eigenvalues are \(\sigma_j^2/n\), and the projected data is \(XV = U\Sigma\). Computing PCA via SVD is more numerically stable than forming the covariance matrix explicitly, and truncated or randomized SVD scales to large data.

q: Why standardize before <abbr title="Principal Component Analysis">PCA</abbr>? How many components do you keep?
a: PCA finds directions of maximum variance, so a feature measured in large units (income in dollars) would dominate one in small units (age in years) purely because of scale. Standardizing puts features on equal footing (unless they share units and their variance is meaningful). Keep enough components to explain about 90–95% of the variance, look for an elbow in the scree plot, or pick the number that maximizes downstream validation performance.

q: Can you trust distances in a t-SNE plot?
a: Not really. t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods, not global geometry: the size of a cluster and the distance between clusters carry little meaning, apparent clusters can appear in structureless data at low perplexity, and the layout changes with perplexity and seed. Use it to explore; validate any claimed clusters with other methods. UMAP preserves somewhat more global structure but has the same caveats.

q: How does Isolation Forest detect anomalies?
a: It builds many random trees, each splitting on a random feature at a random threshold. Anomalies are few and different, so random splits isolate them in few steps (short paths from the root), while normal points sit in dense regions and need many splits. The anomaly score is based on the average path length across trees, normalized by the expected path length for a dataset of that size. It's fast, scales linearly, and needs no distance metric.

q: How do you evaluate an unsupervised model in practice?
a: Use internal metrics (silhouette, Davies–Bouldin) to compare settings; check stability across seeds and subsamples; compare with any available labels (ARI, NMI) or with human review of samples from each cluster; and most importantly measure the downstream effect: whether segments behave differently, whether flagged anomalies are confirmed by investigators (precision@k), or whether features derived from clusters improve a supervised model.

q: Collaborative filtering vs content-based filtering.
a: Collaborative filtering uses only interaction patterns (users who liked X also liked Y); it discovers non-obvious relationships and needs no item features, but fails on new users and items (cold start) and favors popular items. Content-based filtering uses item and user features; it works for new items and niche interests but needs good features and tends to recommend more of the same. Production systems are hybrids, for example two-tower models that include both IDs and content features.

q: Explain matrix factorization for recommendations.
a: Represent each user and item by a \(k\)-dimensional vector so that their dot product (plus biases) predicts the interaction. Learn the vectors by minimizing squared error on observed entries with L2 regularization, using SGD or alternating least squares. The low rank forces the model to find latent factors (genre, style, price level) shared across users and items, which generalizes to unobserved pairs.

q: How do you handle cold start?
a: New users: popular or trending items, items popular in their context (location, device, traffic source), a short onboarding to collect preferences, and quick adaptation from the first few interactions in the session. New items: content-based embeddings (text, image, metadata) so the item tower can embed them without history, creator or category priors, and exploration slots (bandits) to gather interactions. Measure cold-start segments separately.

q: Why use candidate generation and ranking as separate stages?
a: Latency and cost. A rich ranking model with hundreds of features can score a few hundred items per request, not millions. Candidate generation uses cheap methods (precomputed item embeddings with approximate nearest-neighbor search, co-visitation lists) optimized for recall, so the ranker only sees plausible items and can optimize precision. Stages also let teams improve retrieval and ranking independently.

q: How is a two-tower model trained and served?
a: Train with positive (user, item) pairs from interactions and negatives from other items in the batch, using a softmax or contrastive loss over dot-product scores, with a correction for item popularity. At serving time, precompute all item embeddings and load them into an approximate nearest-neighbor index; compute the user embedding per request from recent features and retrieve the top items by dot product. Rebuild the index regularly to include new items.

q: What is position bias and how do you correct for it?
a: Items shown higher get more clicks regardless of relevance, so naive training on click logs learns "position" rather than quality and reinforces the existing ranking. Corrections: include position as a feature during training and set it to a constant at serving; inverse propensity weighting using click-propensity estimates per position (from randomized experiments); and occasional randomized ordering to measure propensities.

q: How do you evaluate a recommender offline and online?
a: Offline, on a time-based split: recall@k and hit rate for retrieval, NDCG or MAP for ranking, plus coverage, diversity and novelty, broken down by user segment (new vs heavy users). Online, with an A/B test: the primary engagement or business metric (watch time, purchases, retention), guardrails (latency, complaints, creator exposure), and long-term holdouts to catch short-term gains that hurt satisfaction.

q: What are feedback loops in recommendation, and why are they dangerous?
a: The model decides what users see, users can only interact with what they see, and the next model trains on those interactions. Items the model ignores never get data, popular items get more popular, and errors compound. Use exploration (a share of traffic for bandit-style exploration or random items), log impressions and propensities, keep a small random holdout to measure true preferences, and diversify.

q: How do you handle implicit feedback with no explicit negatives?
a: Treat interactions as positives with confidence weights (watch time, repeat purchases), and sample negatives: random items, in-batch negatives, or impressions the user saw but skipped (the most informative). Use ranking losses (BPR, sampled softmax) instead of rating regression. Account for exposure: an item never shown is unknown, not disliked.

q: Design a 'people you may know' or 'similar items' feature.
a: Candidates from graph signals (friends of friends, shared groups or contacts) or from co-interaction and embedding similarity for items; rank with features such as mutual connections, interaction recency, embedding similarity and context, trained on accept or click labels; re-rank for diversity and privacy rules; evaluate offline with recall@k and AUC on a time split, online with acceptance rate and downstream engagement; guard against privacy harms (don't surface sensitive connections) and feedback loops.

q: Why can't a single perceptron learn XOR?
a: A perceptron's decision boundary is a single line (hyperplane). XOR's positive points (0,1) and (1,0) sit on one diagonal and the negatives (0,0) and (1,1) on the other, so no single line separates them. One hidden layer fixes it: two hidden units can compute OR and NAND (or AND), and the output combines them, which is exactly the feature engineering a linear model can't do for itself.

q: Why do neural networks need non-linear activations?
a: Without them, a stack of linear layers is just one linear map, \(W_n \cdots W_1 x\), so depth adds no expressive power and the network can only represent linear functions. The non-linearity between layers lets each layer bend and fold the space so later layers can separate classes that weren't linearly separable.

q: What does the universal approximation theorem say, and what doesn't it say?
a: One hidden layer with enough units and a suitable non-linearity can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain arbitrarily well. It doesn't say how many units are needed (possibly exponentially many), that gradient descent will find the weights, or that the network will generalize from finite data. Deep networks achieve the same with far fewer parameters by composing features.

q: Derive backpropagation for a two-layer network.
a: With \(Z_1 = XW_1 + b_1\), \(A_1 = \text{ReLU}(Z_1)\), \(Z_2 = A_1W_2 + b_2\) and softmax cross-entropy: \(\partial Z_2 = (P - Y)/n\); \(\partial W_2 = A_1^\top \partial Z_2\); \(\partial b_2 = \sum_{\text{rows}} \partial Z_2\); \(\partial A_1 = \partial Z_2 W_2^\top\); \(\partial Z_1 = \partial A_1 \odot \mathbb{1}[Z_1 > 0]\); \(\partial W_1 = X^\top \partial Z_1\); \(\partial b_1 = \sum_{\text{rows}} \partial Z_1\). State shapes as you go; a shape mismatch is the fastest way to catch an error.

q: Why is backpropagation efficient compared with computing each gradient separately?
a: It reuses intermediate results. The gradient flowing into each layer is computed once and shared by all parameters below it, so the total cost is a small constant multiple (about 2–3×) of a forward pass, regardless of how many parameters there are. Finite differences would need one or two forward passes per parameter, which is impossible for millions or billions of parameters.

q: Why does backprop need to store activations, and what is gradient checkpointing?
a: The gradient of a layer's weights depends on that layer's input (\(\partial W = A^\top \partial Z\)) and activation derivatives depend on pre-activations, so the forward values must be kept until the backward pass reaches that layer. Memory grows with depth, batch size and sequence length. Gradient checkpointing stores activations only at some layers and recomputes the others during the backward pass, trading extra compute for a large memory saving; it's standard in LLM training.

q: Why does sigmoid cause vanishing gradients?
a: Its derivative \(\sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x))\) is at most 0.25 (at \(x = 0\)) and close to 0 when the unit saturates. Backprop multiplies one such factor per layer, so gradients shrink exponentially with depth; the early layers barely learn. It's also not zero-centered, which makes gradient updates zig-zag. Hidden layers therefore use ReLU-family activations, and sigmoid stays at outputs and inside gates.

q: Why <abbr title="Rectified Linear Unit">ReLU</abbr> over sigmoid in hidden layers?
a: ReLU's gradient is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so it doesn't shrink gradients through active units; it's very cheap to compute; and it produces sparse activations. That made deep networks much faster to train (AlexNet reported several times faster convergence than tanh). Its weakness is dying units; Leaky ReLU, ELU or GELU address that.

q: What is the dying <abbr title="Rectified Linear Unit">ReLU</abbr> problem and how do you fix it?
a: If a unit's pre-activation becomes negative for every input (for example after a large update or with a large negative bias), its output and gradient are zero forever, so it never recovers. Fixes: Leaky ReLU or PReLU (small slope for negative inputs), ELU or GELU, lower learning rates, He initialization, and normalization layers.

q: Why do LLMs use <abbr title="Gaussian Error Linear Unit">GELU</abbr> or SwiGLU instead of <abbr title="Rectified Linear Unit">ReLU</abbr>?
a: Smooth activations give smoother loss surfaces and keep small gradients for negative inputs, and empirically they train Transformers to lower loss. SwiGLU, a gated linear unit using SiLU, adds a multiplicative gate inside the feed-forward layer, which performed best in Shazeer's comparison of GLU variants and was adopted by PaLM and LLaMA. To keep parameter count equal, the hidden width is usually reduced from \(4d\) to about \(\tfrac{8}{3}d\).

q: Why not initialize all weights to zero?
a: All units in a layer would receive identical inputs, compute identical outputs and get identical gradients, so they would remain identical: the layer behaves like a single unit (the symmetry problem). Random initialization breaks the symmetry. Biases can start at zero.

q: Xavier vs He initialization.
a: Both pick the weight variance so activations and gradients keep roughly constant variance across layers. Xavier uses \(\frac{2}{n_{in} + n_{out}}\), derived for symmetric activations like tanh. He uses \(\frac{2}{n_{in}}\), accounting for ReLU zeroing about half of its inputs, which halves the variance. Using Xavier with deep ReLU networks makes activations shrink layer by layer.

q: Why subtract the maximum before computing softmax?
a: \(e^{z}\) overflows for large logits (above about 88 in float32). Softmax is unchanged by subtracting a constant from every logit, so subtracting the maximum makes the largest exponent \(e^0 = 1\) and all others smaller, avoiding overflow. For the loss, use log-softmax with the log-sum-exp trick so you never take the log of an underflowed zero.

q: How do you detect and fix exploding gradients?
a: Symptoms: loss suddenly becomes NaN or spikes, very large gradient norms, weights blowing up. Monitor the global gradient norm per step. Fixes: gradient clipping by global norm (commonly 1.0), a lower learning rate or warmup, better initialization, normalization layers, residual connections, and checking the data for extreme values or bad labels.

q: Reverse-mode vs forward-mode automatic differentiation.
a: Reverse mode (backprop) computes the gradient of one output with respect to all inputs in one backward pass, ideal when the output is a scalar loss and the inputs are billions of parameters. Forward mode carries derivatives forward alongside values, one input direction per pass, which is efficient for functions with few inputs and many outputs. Jacobian–vector products use forward mode and vector–Jacobian products use reverse mode.

q: Explain Adam step by step.
a: Adam keeps two exponential moving averages per parameter: \(m\) of the gradient (momentum, direction) and \(v\) of the squared gradient (scale). Both start at zero, so it divides them by \(1 - \beta_1^t\) and \(1 - \beta_2^t\) to correct the bias in early steps. The update is \(\eta\,\hat m / (\sqrt{\hat v} + \epsilon)\): parameters with consistently large gradients take relatively smaller steps, and rarely updated ones take larger steps. Defaults are \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.999\), \(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\).

q: Why AdamW instead of Adam with L2 regularization?
a: In Adam, an L2 penalty's gradient \(\lambda\theta\) is added to the loss gradient and then divided by \(\sqrt{\hat v}\), so weights with large gradient history are regularized less, which isn't what weight decay is supposed to do. AdamW decouples it: it applies \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\lambda\theta\) directly, independent of the adaptive scaling. This generalizes better and makes the learning rate and decay strength easier to tune separately.

q: Momentum: what problem does it solve?
a: In a long, narrow valley, gradients point mostly across the valley, so SGD bounces between the walls while making slow progress along the floor. Momentum keeps a running average of gradients: oscillating components cancel and the consistent component accumulates, so the optimizer speeds up along the valley and damps the zig-zag. It also helps pass through small bumps and plateaus.

q: Why use learning-rate warmup for Transformers?
a: At the start, weights are random and Adam's second-moment estimate \(v\) is based on very few gradients, so the effective per-parameter step sizes can be huge and unstable. Large early updates, combined with LayerNorm and attention softmax, can push training into divergence or a bad region. Ramping the learning rate up over the first steps lets the statistics stabilize. Pre-LN architectures need less warmup than Post-LN, but warmup is still standard.

q: What is the relationship between batch size and learning rate?
a: Bigger batches give lower-variance gradient estimates, so you can take larger steps. For SGD, the linear scaling rule (scale the rate with the batch, plus warmup) works up to a critical batch size; beyond it, returns diminish. Adaptive optimizers often scale closer to the square root. Very large batches may need retuning (LARS/LAMB) to avoid a generalization gap. When you change one, retune the other.

q: How much memory does Adam need for a 7B-parameter model?
a: In mixed-precision training with fp32 optimizer states: BF16 weights (2 bytes) + BF16 gradients (2) + an fp32 master copy of weights (4) + Adam's \(m\) (4) and \(v\) (4) = about 16 bytes per parameter, so roughly 112 GB for 7B parameters, before activations. That's why full fine-tuning needs multiple GPUs or sharding (ZeRO/FSDP), and why LoRA and 8-bit optimizers are popular.

q: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm: why do Transformers use LayerNorm?
a: BatchNorm normalizes each feature across the batch, so its output depends on other examples in the batch, it needs running statistics at inference, and it breaks down with small batches and variable-length sequences. LayerNorm normalizes across the features of each token independently: no batch dependence, identical behavior in training and inference, and it works for autoregressive generation one token at a time. Many LLMs use RMSNorm, a cheaper LayerNorm without mean subtraction.

q: How does BatchNorm behave at inference time?
a: During training it normalizes with the current batch's mean and variance and updates exponential moving averages of them. At inference (model.eval()) it uses those running averages, so outputs don't depend on the batch. Forgetting to switch to eval mode, or training with tiny batches so the running statistics are poor, causes a training–inference mismatch.

q: Pre-LN vs Post-LN Transformers.
a: Post-LN applies normalization after the residual addition: \(\text{Norm}(x + F(x))\). Gradients near the output are large and those to early layers can be unstable, so deep Post-LN models need careful warmup. Pre-LN normalizes the sublayer input: \(x + F(\text{Norm}(x))\), leaving an un-normalized identity path from input to output, which keeps gradients well-behaved and trains deep stacks more reliably. Most modern LLMs use Pre-LN (often with RMSNorm), plus a final normalization before the output layer.

q: How does dropout work at training vs test time?
a: During training, each unit is zeroed with probability \(p\) and the survivors are scaled by \(1/(1-p)\) (inverted dropout), so expected activations stay the same. At test time dropout is disabled and no scaling is needed. It prevents co-adaptation of units and approximates averaging an ensemble of thinned networks. Monte Carlo dropout keeps it on at inference to estimate uncertainty.

q: Why do large LLMs use little or no dropout?
a: Pretraining datasets are so large that the model sees most tokens about once, so classic overfitting is rarely the bottleneck; underfitting is. Dropout also slows convergence and wastes compute at that scale. Fine-tuning on small datasets may still use dropout, along with weight decay and early stopping.

q: What is label smoothing and why does it help?
a: Instead of training toward a one-hot target, you train toward \(1 - \epsilon\) for the correct class and \(\epsilon/(K-1)\) for the others. It discourages logits from growing without bound, reduces over-confidence, improves calibration and sometimes accuracy. Downsides: it can hurt knowledge distillation (smoothed teachers carry less information) and it slightly changes the meaning of predicted probabilities.

q: Your training loss is NaN. How do you debug it?
a: Find the first step where it happens and log the loss, gradient norms and activations around it. Common causes: learning rate too high or no warmup, no gradient clipping, FP16 overflow (use BF16 or loss scaling), log of zero or division by zero in a custom loss, exploding attention logits, and bad input values (NaN or infinities in data). Fix by lowering the rate, adding warmup and clipping, using numerically stable functions (log-softmax, BCE with logits), and validating the data pipeline.

q: How do you know your model can learn at all?
a: Check that the initial loss is near \(\ln K\) for \(K\) classes, then try to overfit a tiny batch (10–100 examples) to near-zero training loss with regularization off. If it can't memorize a few examples, there's a bug: labels misaligned, the loss applied to the wrong tensor, gradients not flowing, or a learning rate that's badly off. Only after that should you tune regularization for generalization.

q: <abbr title="Stochastic Gradient Descent">SGD</abbr> vs Adam: when would you choose <abbr title="Stochastic Gradient Descent">SGD</abbr>?
a: Adam converges faster with less tuning and is the default for Transformers, sparse features and NLP. Well-tuned SGD with momentum and a good schedule often matches or slightly beats Adam on image classification with CNNs, sometimes generalizing better, and uses less memory (one state per parameter instead of two). Choose SGD for CNN vision baselines with established recipes or tight memory; Adam/AdamW otherwise.

q: What is gradient accumulation?
a: When a desired batch doesn't fit in memory, run several smaller micro-batches, sum (or average) their gradients without stepping the optimizer, then take one step. Mathematically it equals training with the larger batch, except for batch-dependent layers like BatchNorm, which still see the small batches. It trades time for memory.

q: Compute the output size and parameter count of a convolutional layer.
a: Output width \(= \lfloor (W - k + 2p)/s \rfloor + 1\) (same for height); output depth is the number of filters \(C_{out}\). Parameters \(= (k \cdot k \cdot C_{in} + 1)\cdot C_{out}\) with biases. Example: 224×224×3 input, 64 filters of 7×7, stride 2, padding 3 → 112×112×64 output with \(7\cdot7\cdot3\cdot64 + 64 = 9{,}472\) parameters. The count doesn't depend on image size; the compute does.

q: Why share weights in a <abbr title="Convolutional Neural Network">CNN</abbr>?
a: It encodes the assumption that a useful pattern (an edge, an eye) can appear anywhere, so the same detector should be applied everywhere. That cuts parameters by orders of magnitude, improves data efficiency because every position provides training signal for the same filter, and makes the layer translation-equivariant.

q: What does a 1×1 convolution do?
a: At each spatial position it computes a linear combination of the input channels, like a dense layer applied per pixel. It changes the number of channels cheaply (bottlenecks in Inception and ResNet), mixes information across channels, and adds a non-linearity when followed by an activation. In depthwise separable convolutions it's the "pointwise" step.

q: Equivariance vs invariance.
a: A function is equivariant to translation if shifting the input shifts the output the same way: convolution feature maps move with the object. It's invariant if shifting the input leaves the output unchanged: a classifier's "cat" score. CNNs are equivariant through convolutions and become approximately invariant through pooling, striding and global average pooling at the end.

q: What is a receptive field and how do you grow it?
a: The region of the input that can influence a given output unit. It grows with depth (each 3×3 layer adds 2 pixels), with stride and pooling (which multiply the growth of later layers), and with dilated convolutions. Large receptive fields are needed for context, such as recognizing large objects or segmenting with scene context. The effective receptive field is usually smaller than the theoretical one and concentrated near the center.

q: Why did AlexNet matter so much?
a: In 2012 it cut ImageNet top-5 error from about 26% to 15.3%, a far larger jump than incremental improvements to hand-crafted features.
