It combined a deep CNN, ReLU (much faster training than tanh), dropout, data augmentation, and training on GPUs with a large labeled dataset. It convinced the field that learned features beat engineered ones given enough data and compute, which started the deep-learning era.

q: Explain the degradation problem and how ResNet solves it.
a: Plain networks deeper than about 20 layers had higher training error than shallower ones, an optimization problem, not overfitting. ResNet adds identity skip connections so each block learns a residual \(F(x)\) and outputs \(F(x) + x\). Learning identity becomes trivial (drive \(F\) toward zero), and gradients flow directly through the skip paths (\(\partial y/\partial x = I + \partial F/\partial x\)). This made 100- to 1000-layer networks trainable.

q: Why use two 3×3 convolutions instead of one 5×5?
a: Same receptive field (5×5), fewer parameters (\(18C^2\) vs \(25C^2\)), and an extra non-linearity between them, which makes the function more expressive. Three 3×3 layers similarly replace a 7×7 (\(27C^2\) vs \(49C^2\)).

q: How much does a depthwise separable convolution save?
a: A standard convolution costs about \(k^2 C_{in} C_{out}\) multiply-adds per position. Depthwise separable splits it into a per-channel \(k \times k\) filter (\(k^2 C_{in}\)) plus a 1×1 pointwise convolution (\(C_{in} C_{out}\)). The ratio is \(\frac{1}{C_{out}} + \frac{1}{k^2}\), so about 8–9 times cheaper for 3×3 kernels, with a small accuracy cost. It's the core of MobileNet and EfficientNet.

q: One-stage vs two-stage object detectors.
a: Two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) first propose candidate regions, then classify and refine each one: more accurate, especially on small objects, but slower. One-stage detectors (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet) predict boxes and classes densely over the image in a single pass: fast enough for real time. RetinaNet's focal loss addressed the extreme foreground–background imbalance that had held one-stage accuracy back.

q: Explain <abbr title="Intersection over Union">IoU</abbr>, non-max suppression and mAP.
a: IoU is the overlap between two boxes divided by their union; a detection usually counts as correct if its IoU with a ground-truth box exceeds 0.5. Non-max suppression keeps the highest-scoring box and removes boxes that overlap it above an IoU threshold, repeating until none remain. mAP computes average precision (the area under the precision–recall curve) per class and averages over classes; COCO averages it over IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 too.

q: Why does U-Net use skip connections?
a: The encoder downsamples to capture context but loses fine spatial detail. Skip connections pass high-resolution feature maps from each encoder level directly to the matching decoder level, where they're concatenated with the upsampled features. The decoder can then produce precise boundaries using both "what" (deep features) and "where" (shallow features). It works well even with small datasets, which is why it's standard in medical imaging.

q: Why does focal loss help RetinaNet?
a: Dense detectors evaluate tens of thousands of candidate locations, nearly all easy background. With cross-entropy, these easy negatives dominate the total loss and gradients. Focal loss multiplies cross-entropy by \((1 - p_t)^\gamma\) (often \(\gamma = 2\)), shrinking the loss for well-classified examples so training concentrates on hard, misclassified ones. Combined with class-balancing weights, it let one-stage detectors match two-stage accuracy.

q: How does <abbr title="Vision Transformer">ViT</abbr> turn an image into tokens, and why does it need so much data?
a: It cuts the image into fixed-size patches (for example 16×16), flattens each and projects it linearly to the model dimension, adds learned position embeddings, prepends a [CLS] token, and feeds the sequence to a Transformer encoder. Unlike a CNN, it has no built-in locality or translation equivariance, so it must learn those regularities from data. With limited data CNNs win; with very large pretraining datasets (or strong augmentation and distillation) ViT matches or beats them.

q: <abbr title="Vision Transformer">ViT</abbr> vs <abbr title="Convolutional Neural Network">CNN</abbr>: which would you choose?
a: For small or medium datasets, edge devices or high-resolution dense prediction with tight compute, a CNN (or a hybrid) is often the better choice. With large pretraining data or a strong pretrained checkpoint, ViTs scale better and integrate naturally with language models. In practice you usually fine-tune a pretrained backbone, and modern CNNs (ConvNeXt) and ViTs perform similarly; choose based on available checkpoints, latency and deployment tooling.

q: Explain the contrastive loss used by SimCLR and CLIP.
a: InfoNCE treats each example as a classification problem: among one positive and many negatives, pick the positive. \(L = -\log\frac{\exp(\text{sim}(q, k^+)/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(\text{sim}(q, k_j)/\tau)}\) with cosine similarity and temperature \(\tau\). SimCLR's positives are two augmented views of one image; CLIP's are an image and its caption, with the loss applied symmetrically in both directions. More negatives give a tighter bound and better representations, hence large batches.

q: How does CLIP do zero-shot classification?
a: Embed each class name in a prompt such as "a photo of a {class}" with the text encoder, embed the image with the image encoder, and predict the class whose text embedding has the highest cosine similarity with the image embedding. No task-specific training is needed, and prompt wording and ensembling prompts change accuracy. Limits: it inherits web-data biases and struggles with counting, fine-grained distinctions and spatial relations.

q: Explain <abbr title="Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency">TF-IDF</abbr> and when <abbr title="Best Matching 25, a keyword ranking function">BM25</abbr> is better.
a: TF-IDF scores a term in a document by its frequency in the document times the log of its inverse document frequency, so terms that are frequent here but rare overall score high. BM25 refines this with term-frequency saturation (repeated occurrences add diminishing value) and normalization by document length relative to the average, with parameters \(k_1\) and \(b\). BM25 ranks better in practice and remains a strong baseline and the keyword component of hybrid search.

q: Skip-gram vs CBOW.
a: Skip-gram predicts each context word from the center word; it learns good vectors for rare words and works well with small data, but is slower. CBOW predicts the center word from the averaged context; it's faster and better for frequent words. Both are trained with negative sampling or hierarchical softmax rather than a full softmax over the vocabulary.

q: What is negative sampling?
a: Computing a softmax over a vocabulary of hundreds of thousands of words for every training pair is expensive. Negative sampling replaces it with binary classification: push up the score of the true (word, context) pair and push down the scores of a few randomly sampled "negative" words, drawn from a smoothed unigram distribution (frequency to the power 0.75). It's cheap and works well, and it's an early example of contrastive learning.

q: Why can't word2vec handle words with several meanings?
a: It learns exactly one vector per word type, regardless of context, so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank account" share one vector that blends both meanings. Contextual models (ELMo, then BERT and GPT) compute a different vector for each occurrence based on the surrounding words.

q: Explain backpropagation through time.
a: Unroll the RNN over the sequence into a deep feed-forward network whose layers share weights, run the forward pass, then backpropagate from the losses at each step back through all time steps, summing the gradient contributions for the shared weights. For long sequences, truncated BPTT backpropagates only through the last \(k\) steps to save memory and compute, at the cost of not learning dependencies longer than \(k\).

q: Why do RNNs have vanishing gradients?
a: The gradient from a late step to an early step is a product of one Jacobian per intervening step, each involving the recurrent weight matrix and the derivative of tanh (at most 1, usually less). If the largest singular value of these factors is below 1, the product shrinks exponentially with distance, so early inputs barely influence learning. Above 1, it explodes. LSTMs, GRUs, careful initialization and gradient clipping address this.

q: Why can't RNNs be parallelized across time?
a: Each hidden state depends on the previous one, \(h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)\), so step \(t\) can't start until step \(t-1\) is finished, during training as well as inference. You can parallelize across the batch but not along the sequence, so training on long sequences is slow and GPUs are underused. Transformers compute all positions at once during training.

q: Walk through each <abbr title="Long Short-Term Memory">LSTM</abbr> gate.
a: The forget gate decides how much of each component of the previous cell state to keep. The input gate decides how much of the new candidate content to write. The candidate is a tanh layer proposing new content. The cell state becomes forget ⊙ old + input ⊙ candidate. The output gate decides how much of the (tanh-squashed) cell state to expose as the hidden state. All gates are sigmoids of the previous hidden state and current input.

q: Why does the <abbr title="Long Short-Term Memory">LSTM</abbr> cell state help gradients flow?
a: The cell state is updated additively: \(c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde c_t\). Its derivative with respect to \(c_{t-1}\) is just \(f_t\), element-wise, with no weight-matrix multiplication or squashing derivative in that path. When forget gates are close to 1, gradients pass through many steps almost unchanged, much like the identity path in a ResNet.

q: What is the parameter count of an <abbr title="Long Short-Term Memory">LSTM</abbr> layer?
a: Four gate blocks (forget, input, candidate, output), each with an input weight matrix \((h \times d)\), a recurrent matrix \((h \times h)\) and a bias \((h)\): \(4(hd + h^2 + h)\). For \(d = h = 256\) that's \(4(65{,}536 + 65{,}536 + 256) = 525{,}312\). A GRU has three blocks, so about \(3/4\) of that.

q: <abbr title="Long Short-Term Memory">LSTM</abbr> vs <abbr title="Gated Recurrent Unit">GRU</abbr>: when would you pick each?
a: They perform similarly on most tasks. GRUs have fewer parameters and train faster, which helps with smaller datasets or tight compute. LSTMs have a separate cell state and an output gate, which can help on tasks needing very precise, long-term memory control. Today both are mostly replaced by Transformers, except in small on-device or streaming models.

q: What are teacher forcing and exposure bias?
a: Teacher forcing feeds the decoder the ground-truth previous token during training, which makes training fast and stable. But at inference the decoder conditions on its own predictions, a distribution it never saw during training, so early mistakes can compound: that mismatch is exposure bias. Mitigations include scheduled sampling, sequence-level training objectives, and, for LLMs, post-training on the model's own generations (RLHF).

q: How did attention fix the seq2seq bottleneck?
a: Instead of compressing the whole source into the final encoder state, the decoder computes, at every step, relevance scores between its current state and every encoder state, normalizes them with softmax, and uses the weighted sum as a context vector. Information about any source word is available directly at every decoding step, so long sentences no longer degrade, and the weights provide an interpretable alignment.

q: Additive vs dot-product attention.
a: Additive (Bahdanau) attention scores with a small feed-forward network, \(v^\top\tanh(W_1 q + W_2 k)\); it works well when query and key dimensions differ and was used first. Dot-product (Luong) attention uses \(q^\top k\) or \(q^\top W k\), which is faster and maps onto efficient matrix multiplication. Transformers use scaled dot-product attention, dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) to stop large dot products from saturating the softmax.

q: Beam search vs greedy decoding.
a: Greedy decoding takes the single most likely token at each step; it's fast but can miss sequences whose first tokens look less likely. Beam search keeps the \(B\) highest-scoring partial sequences at each step and returns the best complete one, usually giving better translations and summaries. It's slower, tends to favor short and generic outputs (so length normalization is used), and is a poor fit for open-ended chat, where sampling gives more natural text.

q: Explain queries, keys and values intuitively.
a: Each token produces three vectors from its embedding. The query says what the token is looking for, each key says what a token can be matched on, and each value is the content a token contributes if attended to. The dot product of a query with every key scores relevance; softmax turns scores into weights; the output is the weighted sum of values. Separating keys from values lets what you match on differ from what you pass along.

q: Why divide by √d_k in attention?
a: For random vectors with unit-variance components, \(q \cdot k\) has variance \(d_k\), so with large head dimensions the raw scores have large magnitude. Softmax of large scores is nearly one-hot, with gradients close to zero, which stalls training. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps the scores' variance around 1 so softmax stays in a range with useful gradients.

q: What are the time and memory costs of self-attention?
a: Computing \(QK^\top\) and multiplying by \(V\) costs \(O(n^2 d)\) time per layer for \(n\) tokens and dimension \(d\), and storing the attention matrix costs \(O(n^2)\) memory per head. Projections and the FFN cost \(O(n d^2)\). So attention dominates for long sequences. In exchange, all positions are processed in parallel and any two tokens interact in one step. FlashAttention removes the \(O(n^2)\) memory without changing the result.

q: What does the causal mask do, and why use −∞ rather than 0?
a: It stops each position from attending to later positions, so during training position \(t\) predicts token \(t+1\) without seeing it, and every position can be trained in parallel. The mask is applied to the scores before softmax: setting a score to \(-\infty\) makes its weight \(e^{-\infty} = 0\) after normalization. Setting the weight to 0 after softmax would break normalization; setting the score to 0 would still give the future token a positive weight.

q: Why use multiple attention heads instead of one big head?
a: One softmax yields a single distribution of attention per token, which must average over all the kinds of relationships at once. Several narrower heads can each attend to different positions for different reasons (previous token, subject of the sentence, matching brackets) and their outputs are combined. Because each head has dimension \(d/h\), the total compute and parameters match one full-width head.

q: How many parameters are in a multi-head attention layer, and in a Transformer block?
a: Attention: \(W_Q\), \(W_K\), \(W_V\) and \(W_O\), each \(d \times d\), so \(4d^2\) (plus \(4d\) for biases if used), independent of the number of heads. FFN with a \(4d\) hidden layer: \(2 \times d \times 4d = 8d^2\). A block is therefore about \(12d^2\), plus small normalization parameters. With grouped-query attention, \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) shrink in proportion to the number of key–value heads.

q: Why does a Transformer need positional encoding?
a: Self-attention treats its input as a set: permuting the tokens permutes the outputs identically, so without position information word order is invisible. Positional encodings inject order, either by adding position vectors to the embeddings (sinusoidal, learned) or by making attention scores depend on relative position (relative biases, RoPE, ALiBi).

q: Explain <abbr title="Rotary Position Embedding">RoPE</abbr> intuitively.
a: RoPE rotates each two-dimensional slice of the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to the token's position, with different slices rotating at different frequencies. A dot product between two rotated vectors depends only on the difference of their angles, so the attention score between positions \(m\) and \(n\) depends on \(m - n\): relative position, encoded without extra parameters and inside the attention computation itself. Context can be extended later by rescaling the frequencies (position interpolation, NTK scaling, YaRN).

q: Compare sinusoidal, learned, <abbr title="Rotary Position Embedding">RoPE</abbr> and <abbr title="Attention with Linear Biases">ALiBi</abbr> positional encodings.
a: Sinusoidal: fixed, added to embeddings, no parameters, weak extrapolation in practice. Learned absolute: a vector per position, flexible, but capped at the trained length. RoPE: rotates queries and keys so scores depend on relative position; the default in modern LLMs; extendable with frequency scaling. ALiBi: adds a linear distance penalty per head to the scores; extrapolates well beyond the training length but imposes a recency bias.

q: What does the feed-forward network in a Transformer block do?
a: It's a two-layer MLP applied to each token independently, usually widening to about \(4d\) with a GELU or SwiGLU non-linearity. Attention mixes information across tokens; the FFN transforms each token's representation, adding non-linear capacity. It holds most of the block's parameters, and interpretability research suggests FFN layers store much factual knowledge as key–value-like associations. MoE layers replace it with many expert FFNs.

q: Why does the Transformer use residual connections and layer normalization?
a: Residual connections give each sublayer an identity path, so gradients reach early layers directly and each sublayer only needs to learn a refinement; without them, deep stacks are very hard to train. Normalization keeps activations at a stable scale across layers, which allows higher learning rates. Pre-LN (normalizing each sublayer's input) preserves a clean residual path and is more stable for deep models than Post-LN.

q: Encoder-only vs decoder-only vs encoder–decoder: when do you use each?
a: Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional context, ideal for classification, entity extraction, embeddings and rerankers; small and fast. Decoder-only (GPT, LLaMA): causal attention and next-token prediction, ideal for generation and general-purpose assistants. Encoder–decoder (T5, BART, Whisper): a bidirectional encoder for the input plus a decoder with cross-attention, strong when input and output are different sequences, as in translation, summarization and speech recognition.

q: Why are most LLMs decoder-only?
a: Next-token prediction turns every token of raw text into a training example and scales smoothly with data and compute. Any task can be phrased as text in, text out, so one model handles everything. The architecture is simpler (one stack, one objective), generation is natural, and the KV cache makes inference efficient. At large scale it matched or beat encoder–decoder models on most tasks, so the field converged on it.

q: What is cross-attention?
a: Attention where the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another. In an encoder–decoder model, each decoder layer has a cross-attention sublayer whose queries come from the decoder's states and whose keys and values come from the encoder's output, letting the decoder consult the source while generating. Multimodal models use the same mechanism to attend from text to image features, and diffusion models use it to condition on text.

q: How does <abbr title="Byte-Pair Encoding">BPE</abbr> tokenization work?
a: Start with a vocabulary of characters (or bytes). Repeatedly find the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens in the training corpus and merge it into a new token, recording the merge, until the vocabulary reaches the target size. To tokenize new text, apply the merges in the learned order. Frequent words become single tokens and rare words split into subwords, so there's no unknown-word problem (with byte-level BPE, any string is representable).

q: Why can LLMs struggle to count the letters in a word?
a: They don't see letters. "strawberry" might be tokenized as two or three subword tokens, so the model must have memorized the spelling of each token to count characters, and that information is only indirectly present in training data. The same applies to digits in arithmetic (numbers split into irregular chunks). Reasoning step by step, spelling the word out, or using a code tool works around it.

q: How does vocabulary size affect a model?
a: A larger vocabulary encodes text in fewer tokens, so more fits in the context window and attention is cheaper per document, and multilingual coverage improves. But the embedding and output matrices grow (\(V \times d\) each), the output softmax costs more, and rare tokens get little training signal. Smaller vocabularies mean longer sequences. Modern LLMs use roughly 32k to 256k tokens.

q: What is weight tying?
a: Using the same matrix for the input token embeddings and the output projection to vocabulary logits (transposed). It saves \(V \times d\) parameters, which is significant for small models with large vocabularies, and often improves quality because both directions learn a shared representation of each token. Larger models often untie them for extra capacity.

q: Estimate the parameter count of a 32-layer Transformer with d = 4096.
a: Each block has about \(12d^2\) parameters (\(4d^2\) attention, \(8d^2\) FFN): \(12 \times 4096^2 \approx 201\) million per layer, so about 6.4 billion for 32 layers. Add embeddings: vocabulary × \(d\), for example \(32{,}000 \times 4096 \approx 131\) million (twice that if the output head is untied). Total about 6.7 billion, matching LLaMA-7B.

q: How many FLOPs does it take to train a model?
a: Roughly \(6N\) FLOPs per training token for \(N\) parameters: about \(2N\) for the forward pass and \(4N\) for the backward pass. So training cost ≈ \(6ND\) for \(D\) tokens. For a 7B model on 2T tokens: \(6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} = 8.4\times10^{22}\) FLOPs. At a sustained \(4\times10^{14}\) FLOP/s per GPU that's about \(2.1\times10^8\) GPU-seconds, roughly 58,000 GPU-hours. This ignores attention's extra cost for long contexts.

q: How is a Transformer trained versus how it generates text?
a: In training, the entire sequence is fed at once and the causal mask lets every position predict its next token in parallel with teacher forcing; the loss is the average cross-entropy. In generation, the model produces one token at a time: run the prompt (prefill), sample a token, append it, and repeat. To avoid recomputing keys and values for all previous tokens at every step, they're cached (KV cache), so each new token costs time proportional to the context length.

q: How does attention compare with convolution and recurrence in its built-in assumptions?
a: Convolution assumes locality and translation equivariance; recurrence assumes sequential order and a compressed running state. Attention assumes almost nothing: any token can interact with any other, with content-dependent weights. That flexibility makes it powerful and general but data-hungry, and position must be added explicitly. With enough data, the weaker assumptions win; with little data, the stronger biases of CNNs or RNNs can help.

q: What are induction heads?
a: A pair of attention heads, often in consecutive layers, that implement "find where the current token appeared before and predict the token that followed it". The first head copies information about the previous token into each position; the second searches for earlier positions whose previous token matches the current one and copies what came next. They appear abruptly during training and are thought to underlie much of in-context learning, such as repeating patterns and copying from the prompt.

q: What is the KV cache and why does it help?
a: During autoregressive generation, each new token attends to all previous tokens' keys and values, which don't change once computed. Caching them per layer means each step only computes the new token's query, key and value and attends over the cache, turning per-token work from re-processing the whole prefix into a single step. The cost is memory that grows linearly with context length and batch size, which often limits how many requests a GPU can serve.

q: Compute the KV-cache size for a model.
a: Multiply 2 (keys and values) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × tokens × batch × bytes per value. For 32 layers, 32 KV heads of size 128 in FP16: \(2 \cdot 32 \cdot 32 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 524{,}288\) bytes, about 0.5 MB per token, so 8,192 tokens × batch 8 ≈ 34 GB. With 8 KV heads (GQA) it's a quarter of that.

q: <abbr title="Multi-Head Attention">MHA</abbr> vs <abbr title="Multi-Query Attention">MQA</abbr> vs <abbr title="Grouped-Query Attention">GQA</abbr>.
a: Multi-head attention gives every query head its own key and value projections: best quality, largest cache. Multi-query attention shares a single key/value head across all query heads: the cache shrinks by the number of heads, decode gets much faster, but quality and training stability can suffer. Grouped-query attention is the middle ground: query heads are split into groups that share K/V (for example 64 query heads, 8 KV heads), giving most of MQA's savings with near-MHA quality. Most current open models use GQA.

q: How does FlashAttention speed up attention without approximating it?
a: Standard attention is limited by memory traffic: it writes and reads the full \(n \times n\) score and probability matrices to and from GPU HBM. FlashAttention tiles \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\) into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM, computes each block's contribution, and combines blocks exactly using an online softmax (running max and sum per row). The full matrix is never materialized, memory becomes \(O(n)\), and the backward pass recomputes blocks instead of storing them. Same result, far fewer memory transfers, several times faster.

q: Prefill vs decode: which is compute-bound and which is memory-bound?
a: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel with large matrix multiplications, so it's compute-bound and drives time-to-first-token. Decode generates one token per step per sequence, reading every weight and the KV cache for a small amount of arithmetic, so it's memory-bandwidth-bound and drives time per output token. Batching helps decode because one weight read serves many sequences; quantization and smaller caches help because fewer bytes move.

q: What is sliding-window attention, and what does it give up?
a: Each token attends only to the previous \(w\) tokens, so cost and KV memory scale with \(nw\) instead of \(n^2\). Information can still travel farther than \(w\) through stacked layers (the receptive field grows by about \(w\) per layer), but distant interactions are indirect and weaker. Some models alternate windowed and full-attention layers to keep exact long-range access.

q: What's the idea behind linear attention, and why isn't it standard?
a: Softmax attention computes \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top)V\), which needs the \(n \times n\) matrix. Linear attention replaces the softmax similarity with a kernel feature map \(\phi\), so \((\phi(Q)\phi(K)^\top)V = \phi(Q)(\phi(K)^\top V)\) can be computed right to left in \(O(n)\), and it can even run as a recurrence. In practice these approximations lose quality, especially on precise retrieval from context, so softmax attention with FlashAttention remains the default, with linear-time layers used in hybrids.

q: What is Mamba, and how does it differ from a Transformer?
a: Mamba is a selective state-space model: a linear recurrence whose parameters depend on the input, so it can decide what to keep in its fixed-size state. It trains in parallel with a hardware-aware scan and runs as a recurrence at inference, giving linear time and constant memory per token with no KV cache. Transformers keep every past token's keys and values and can look any of them up exactly, which makes them better at copying and precise recall; hybrids combine a few attention layers with many Mamba layers.

q: How do models extend their context length?
a: Architecturally, with RoPE scaling (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) so positions beyond the trained range map onto rotations the model has seen, followed by fine-tuning on long sequences. Systems-wise, with FlashAttention, context parallelism for training, and KV-cache paging, quantization or eviction for serving. And practically by evaluating long-context use, since models often under-use information in the middle of long prompts.

q: How does mixture-of-experts routing work?
a: A router (a linear layer plus softmax) scores all experts for each token, the top-\(k\) experts process it, and their outputs are combined with the router weights. Only those \(k\) experts' FFN weights are used for that token. An auxiliary load-balancing loss or bias adjustment keeps tokens spread across experts, and a capacity limit caps tokens per expert per batch.

q: Why does <abbr title="Mixture of Experts">MoE</abbr> need a load-balancing mechanism?
a: Routing is learned, and early on some experts happen to perform slightly better, receive more tokens, improve further, and attract even more: a rich-get-richer collapse where a few experts do everything and the rest stay untrained. Imbalance also overloads some GPUs while others idle. A balancing loss (penalizing uneven token fractions and router probabilities) or per-expert bias adjustments keep utilization even.

q: Total vs active parameters in <abbr title="Mixture of Experts">MoE</abbr>: which determines memory and which determines speed?
a: Memory is set by total parameters: every expert must be loaded somewhere, so a 47B-total MoE needs memory like a 47B dense model. Compute per token is set by active parameters: each token uses only its top-\(k\) experts plus shared layers, so it runs roughly like a 13B dense model. Serving MoEs therefore needs large memory but gives high throughput per FLOP, especially at large batch sizes.

q: What is the 'lost in the middle' problem?
a: When relevant information is placed in the middle of a long prompt, models retrieve and use it less reliably than when it's near the beginning or end. It shows that a large context window isn't the same as using all of it well. Mitigations: put the most important content at the start or end, retrieve less but better, summarize, and evaluate long-context tasks directly.

q: Explain the causal language modeling objective.
a: Given a sequence \(x_1 \dots x_T\), train the model to maximize \(\sum_t \log P(x_t \mid x_{<t})\): at every position, predict the next token from everything before it. With a causal mask, all positions train in parallel from one forward pass. It's self-supervised, so any text is training data, and it's equivalent to minimizing cross-entropy between the model's next-token distribution and the actual next token.

q: Explain BERT's masked language modeling and the 80/10/10 rule.
a: BERT selects 15% of input tokens and trains the encoder to predict them using context from both sides. Of the selected tokens, 80% become [MASK], 10% become a random token and 10% stay unchanged. Because [MASK] never appears during fine-tuning or real use, always masking would create a train–test mismatch; mixing in random and unchanged tokens forces the model to build good representations for every position, not just masked ones.

q: BERT vs GPT: objectives and uses.
a: BERT is an encoder trained with masked language modeling: bidirectional context, excellent representations for classification, extraction, embeddings and reranking, but no natural way to generate. GPT is a decoder trained with next-token prediction: causal context, naturally generative, and at scale capable of in-context learning across tasks. Today GPT-style models are the general-purpose LLMs, while BERT-style encoders remain efficient specialists.

q: Why was next-sentence prediction dropped in RoBERTa?
a: Ablations showed NSP didn't help and sometimes hurt downstream performance. The task was too easy: negative pairs came from different documents, so the model could solve it from topic differences rather than coherence. RoBERTa instead trained longer, on more data, with larger batches and dynamic masking, on full sentences packed into long sequences, and did better.

q: What changed architecturally from GPT-2 to LLaMA?
a: The core decoder-only Transformer stayed the same; the components were modernized: Pre-LN with RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm, SwiGLU feed-forward layers instead of GELU MLPs, rotary position embeddings instead of learned absolute positions, no bias terms, and in later versions grouped-query attention and much larger vocabularies. The bigger change was training: far more tokens per parameter on carefully filtered data.

q: What did Chinchilla change?
a: It showed that for a fixed training compute budget (\(C \approx 6ND\)), parameters and training tokens should grow roughly equally, about 20 tokens per parameter, and that models like GPT-3 and Gopher were undertrained. Chinchilla, 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens, outperformed the 280B Gopher with the same compute and was cheaper to serve. It shifted the field toward training smaller models on much more data.

q: Why train small models on far more tokens than the compute-optimal amount?
a: Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute for a target loss. But total cost includes inference, which scales with model size and with how many tokens are served. A smaller model trained much longer reaches a similar loss with higher training cost but far lower serving cost, latency and memory, and fits on cheaper hardware or devices. For widely deployed models that trade is worth it.

q: Estimate the training compute for a 7B model on 2 trillion tokens.
a: Use \(C \approx 6ND = 6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} = 8.4\times10^{22}\) FLOPs. If a GPU sustains about \(4\times10^{14}\) FLOP/s (around 40% utilization of a modern accelerator's BF16 peak), that's \(2.1\times10^8\) GPU-seconds, about 58,000 GPU-hours, or roughly 25 days on 100 GPUs.

q: How is pretraining data cleaned?
a: Start from web crawls, code, books and papers; identify language; apply heuristic filters (length, symbol and repetition ratios, boilerplate removal); score quality with classifiers or reference-model perplexity; deduplicate exactly and approximately (MinHash/LSH), which reduces memorization and wasted compute; filter unsafe content and personal information; remove benchmark test sets (decontamination); then set mixture weights across sources, often with a final high-quality annealing phase.

q: What is in-context learning?
a: The ability of a pretrained model to perform a task described in the prompt, from instructions and a few examples, without changing its weights. Its performance depends on model scale and on the examples' selection, order and format. Proposed explanations include induction heads that copy patterns, implicit inference of the task, and attention implementing learning-like updates over the examples.

q: Few-shot prompting vs fine-tuning: trade-offs.
a: Few-shot prompting needs no training, adapts instantly and keeps one model for many tasks, but uses context window space and tokens on every call, is sensitive to example choice, and is capped by what the base model can already do. Fine-tuning bakes the behavior into the weights: shorter prompts, more consistent format, often a smaller and cheaper model, and better results with enough data, at the cost of a training pipeline, data collection and maintenance.

q: Are emergent abilities real?
a: Some abilities appear to jump from near-random to good at a certain scale. Later analysis showed many of these jumps come from discontinuous metrics like exact match: measured with continuous metrics such as token-level log-likelihood, improvement is often smooth and predictable. Capabilities still do improve with scale, and some practically useful behaviors only become reliable past certain sizes, but "sudden emergence" is often a measurement artifact.

q: Top-k vs top-p sampling.
a: Top-k samples from a fixed number of the most likely tokens, regardless of how confident the model is: too many candidates when the distribution is peaked, too few when it's flat. Top-p (nucleus) sampling takes the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches \(p\), so the candidate set shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it isn't. They're often combined, together with temperature.

q: What does temperature do mathematically?
a: It divides the logits before the softmax: \(p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)}\). \(T < 1\) exaggerates differences between logits, concentrating probability on the top tokens (as \(T \to 0\) it becomes greedy). \(T > 1\) shrinks differences, flattening the distribution and increasing diversity and the chance of unlikely tokens. \(T = 1\) is the model's own distribution.

q: Why is beam search a poor fit for chat?
a: Beam search seeks the highest-probability sequence, and the highest-probability text is often short, generic and repetitive, unlike how people write. It's also slower and reduces diversity. For open-ended generation, sampling with temperature and top-p produces more natural and varied responses; beam search still suits tasks with one correct output, such as translation.

q: How do you force an <abbr title="Large Language Model">LLM</abbr> to produce valid JSON?
a: Strongest: constrained decoding, where at each step tokens that would violate the JSON schema or grammar are masked out, so the output is guaranteed parseable (structured-output features in model APIs, or libraries that compile a schema into a grammar). Weaker: clear instructions with a schema and examples, tool or function-calling interfaces, then validating, and retrying with the error message on failure.

q: Why do LLMs hallucinate?
a: They're trained to produce likely continuations, not verified facts, so when knowledge is missing or uncertain they still generate fluent, plausible text. Causes include gaps and errors in training data, knowledge cutoffs, sampling randomness, preference training that rewards confident or agreeable answers, and evaluations that reward guessing over abstaining. Hallucination is a property of the objective, so it can be reduced and measured but not eliminated.

q: How would you reduce hallucinations in a production chatbot?
a: Ground answers in retrieved documents and require citations; instruct and allow the model to say it doesn't know; use tools for facts and arithmetic; lower temperature; validate outputs (schema checks, entailment checks between answer and sources, a verifier model); fine-tune on examples of abstaining; restrict scope to supported topics; and measure the hallucination rate on a labeled evaluation set drawn from real traffic, tracking it in production with user feedback.

q: How do you measure hallucination?
a: Build an evaluation set representative of real questions with known answers or source documents. For grounded tasks, measure faithfulness: whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, using human labels or an LLM judge calibrated against humans. For open questions, measure factual accuracy against references, and track abstention rates (a model that never answers never hallucinates). Report by category and monitor in production through sampling and user flags.

q: When would you fine-tune instead of using <abbr title="Retrieval-Augmented Generation">RAG</abbr> or prompting?
a: Fine-tune when you need to change how the model behaves: a consistent output format, tone or persona, domain-specific language, following a complex policy, reliable tool use, or a smaller, cheaper model for a narrow task. Use RAG when the problem is what the model knows: private, large or frequently changing information that needs citations and access control. Try prompting first, measure on an evaluation set, and combine approaches (a fine-tuned model that also uses RAG) when needed.

q: Explain <abbr title="Low-Rank Adaptation">LoRA</abbr> and why B is initialized to zero.
a: LoRA freezes a pretrained weight \(W_0\) and learns a low-rank update \(\Delta W = \frac{\alpha}{r}BA\), with \(B\) of shape \((d, r)\) and \(A\) of shape \((r, k)\) and \(r\) small, so only \(r(d + k)\) parameters train. \(A\) starts random and \(B\) starts at zero so that \(\Delta W = 0\) initially: the model starts exactly at the pretrained behavior and the adapter learns only the change. If both were random, training would start from a randomly perturbed model.

q: Why does <abbr title="Low-Rank Adaptation">LoRA</abbr> add no inference latency?
a: After training, \(\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\) is a matrix of the same shape as \(W_0\), so you can add it once: \(W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA\). The deployed model has exactly the original architecture and cost. Adapters, by contrast, insert extra layers that run on every forward pass. You can also keep LoRA weights separate to swap them per request, which adds a small cost but lets many tasks share one base model.

q: What does <abbr title="Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation">QLoRA</abbr> quantize, and what stays in higher precision?
a: The frozen base model's weights are stored in 4-bit NF4 (with double-quantized scales). The LoRA adapter weights, their gradients and optimizer states stay in 16-bit (BF16), and computation happens in BF16 by dequantizing each weight block on the fly. Gradients flow through the frozen 4-bit weights into the adapters, but the 4-bit weights are never updated.

q: How do you choose the <abbr title="Low-Rank Adaptation">LoRA</abbr> rank?
a: Start around 8–16 for style and format changes and 32–64 or more for larger domain shifts or harder tasks; apply LoRA to all linear layers rather than only attention, which often matters more than rank. Tune rank, alpha (often set to 2× rank or equal to rank) and learning rate together, and compare against full fine-tuning on a validation set if the shift is large. Too high a rank on little data can overfit.

q: How much memory do you need to fully fine-tune a 7B model?
a: About 16 bytes per parameter with Adam in mixed precision (2 for BF16 weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for FP32 master weights, 8 for Adam's two moments), so roughly 112 GB, plus activations that depend on batch size and sequence length. That needs several GPUs with ZeRO/FSDP sharding, or tricks like 8-bit optimizers and gradient checkpointing. LoRA cuts it to roughly the 14 GB BF16 base plus small extras; QLoRA to around 4–6 GB for the base.

q: How much memory does a 70B model need in <abbr title="16-bit floating point">FP16</abbr> vs INT4?
a: Weights alone: 70B × 2 bytes ≈ 140 GB in FP16, about 70 GB in 8-bit, and about 35 GB in 4-bit (plus a few percent for quantization scales). On top of that you need KV-cache memory, which grows with context length and batch size, and some activation workspace. So FP16 needs at least two 80 GB GPUs, while a 4-bit version can fit on one 48 GB or 80 GB GPU with room for the cache.

q: Post-training quantization vs quantization-aware training.
a: PTQ quantizes an already-trained model using a small calibration set, with no retraining: fast and cheap, and good at 8 bits and usually acceptable at 4 bits with methods like GPTQ or AWQ. QAT simulates quantization during training (with straight-through gradient estimates) so the weights adapt to the rounding: better quality at very low bit widths, but it needs a training pipeline and compute. Most LLM deployments use PTQ.

q: Why do activation outliers make <abbr title="Large Language Model">LLM</abbr> quantization hard?
a: In large Transformers, a few hidden dimensions take on values far larger than the rest. With one scale per tensor or per row, those outliers force a huge scale, so all the normal values collapse into a handful of integer levels and lose precision. Solutions: keep outlier dimensions in higher precision (LLM.int8), use finer-grained scales (per-channel or per-group), or move the difficulty into the weights by rescaling (SmoothQuant, AWQ).

q: Weight-only vs weight-and-activation quantization.
a: Weight-only quantization (for example 4-bit weights with 16-bit compute) shrinks memory and speeds up memory-bound decoding, because fewer bytes stream from memory, but matrix multiplications still run in 16-bit after dequantization. Weight-and-activation quantization (W8A8 or FP8) also runs the matrix multiplications in low precision on hardware that supports it, speeding up compute-bound phases such as prefill and large-batch serving, but activations are harder to quantize accurately.

q: Why use a temperature in knowledge distillation?
a: A confident teacher assigns nearly all probability to the top class, so its outputs carry little more information than hard labels. Dividing logits by \(T > 1\) softens the distribution and reveals relative similarities among the wrong classes ("dark knowledge"), which is a richer training signal for the student. The KL term is multiplied by \(T^2\) because softening shrinks gradients by about \(1/T^2\).

q: Structured vs unstructured pruning.
a: Unstructured pruning removes individual weights (for example the smallest magnitudes), reaching high sparsity with little accuracy loss, but irregular sparsity only speeds things up with specialized kernels or hardware (such as 2:4 sparsity). Structured pruning removes whole units, heads, channels or layers, so the smaller model is dense and faster everywhere, at a larger accuracy cost that usually needs fine-tuning or distillation to recover.

q: How would you shrink a model to run on a phone?
a: Pick a small, capable base model, distill it from a larger teacher on your task, quantize to 8-bit or 4-bit with calibration data (or QAT if quality drops), prune or remove layers if needed, compile it with a mobile runtime, and evaluate accuracy, latency, memory and battery on real devices. Keep a server fallback for hard cases.

q: <abbr title="bfloat16, a 16-bit float with FP32's exponent range">BF16</abbr> vs <abbr title="16-bit floating point">FP16</abbr>.
a: Both use 16 bits. FP16 has 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits: more precision but a small range, so gradients can underflow and training needs loss scaling. BF16 has 8 exponent bits (the same range as FP32) and 7 mantissa bits: less precision but no overflow or underflow issues in practice, so no loss scaling. BF16 is the standard for training large models on hardware that supports it.

q: <abbr title="Distributed Data Parallel">DDP</abbr> vs <abbr title="Fully Sharded Data Parallel">FSDP</abbr>/ZeRO.
a: DDP replicates the full model, gradients and optimizer state on every GPU and all-reduces gradients each step; it's simple and fast but limited to models whose full training state fits on one GPU. ZeRO and FSDP shard optimizer states, gradients and, at stage 3, parameters across the data-parallel GPUs, gathering each layer's parameters just in time for its computation. Memory per GPU drops roughly in proportion to the number of GPUs, at the cost of more communication.

q: Tensor vs pipeline parallelism, and what is the pipeline bubble?
a: Tensor parallelism splits individual matrices across GPUs, so each layer's computation is shared; it communicates inside every layer and needs very fast links, so it's used within a node. Pipeline parallelism puts different layers on different GPUs and passes activations between stages; communication is lighter, so it works across nodes, but GPUs idle while the pipeline fills and drains: that idle time is the bubble. Splitting batches into many micro-batches and interleaving schedules shrinks it.

q: What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you limit it when fine-tuning?
a: Fine-tuning on a narrow dataset can overwrite general capabilities the model had, such as reasoning, other languages or safety behavior. Limit it with PEFT (LoRA keeps base weights frozen), lower learning rates and fewer epochs, mixing some general or original-task data into the fine-tuning set, regularizing toward the original weights, and evaluating general benchmarks alongside the target task.

q: Prefill vs decode: what's the difference, and which is the bottleneck?
a: Prefill processes all prompt tokens at once to build the KV cache and produce the first token; it's dominated by large matrix multiplications, so it's compute-bound and determines time to first token. Decode generates tokens one at a time; each step reads all the weights and the KV cache for a small amount of arithmetic, so it's memory-bandwidth-bound and determines time per token. Long prompts hurt TTFT; long outputs hurt total latency.

q: What is continuous batching and why does it matter?
a: Instead of running a fixed batch until every sequence finishes, the scheduler updates the batch at each decode step: finished sequences leave and waiting requests join immediately. GPUs stay full despite very different output lengths, and short requests don't wait for long ones. It's one of the largest throughput wins in LLM serving and is standard in vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and SGLang.

q: Explain PagedAttention.
a: Naive servers reserve a contiguous KV-cache region per sequence sized for the maximum length, wasting most of it through over-reservation and fragmentation. PagedAttention splits the cache into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand and tracked with a block table, like virtual-memory pages, and the attention kernel reads keys and values from non-contiguous blocks. Waste drops to near zero, many more sequences fit in memory (higher batch sizes and throughput), and blocks can be shared across sequences, for example for common prefixes or parallel sampling.

q: How does speculative decoding keep the output identical in distribution?
a: A draft model proposes tokens; the target model computes its own probabilities for all of them in one pass. Each draft token \(x\) is accepted with probability \(\min(1, p_{target}(x)/p_{draft}(x))\); at the first rejection, a token is sampled from the normalized residual \(\max(0, p_{target} - p_{draft})\) and the rest of the draft is discarded. This rejection-sampling scheme provably yields samples from exactly the target distribution, so speed improves without changing quality; the speed-up depends on the acceptance rate.

q: What limits decode speed at batch size 1, and how do you estimate it?
a: Memory bandwidth. Each token requires reading all model weights (plus the KV cache) from GPU memory, so the minimum time per token is roughly model bytes ÷ bandwidth. A 7B FP16 model (14 GB) on a GPU with about 3 TB/s is limited to about 210 tokens per second; quantizing to 4 bits raises the ceiling about fourfold. Batching amortizes the weight reads across sequences, which is why throughput grows with batch size.

q: What's the difference between latency and throughput in <abbr title="Large Language Model">LLM</abbr> serving, and how do you trade them off?
a: Latency is how fast one request completes (TTFT and time per token); throughput is total tokens per second across all users. Larger batches raise throughput and lower cost per token but increase each request's per-token latency and queueing. Set latency targets (p95 TTFT and inter-token latency), then maximize goodput, the throughput that meets those targets, with batching, chunked prefill, and separate pools for latency-sensitive and batch traffic.

q: What is prefix caching and when does it help?
a: Reusing the KV cache for a shared beginning of the prompt instead of recomputing prefill. It helps when many requests share long prefixes: system prompts, tool definitions, few-shot examples, the same document in a RAG or agent loop, and multi-turn chats where each turn resends history. It cuts TTFT and cost substantially. Put stable content first and variable content last so prefixes actually match.

q: What is semantic caching, and what are its risks?
a: Storing previous responses keyed by an embedding of the request and returning a cached answer when a new request is similar enough. It saves cost and latency for repetitive queries. Risks: returning a wrong answer for a subtly different question (the similarity threshold matters), stale answers when data changes, and leaking personalized or permissioned answers across users. Scope caches by user or tenant, set expiry, and evaluate the false-hit rate.

q: How would you serve 50 fine-tuned variants of one base model?
a: Fine-tune them as LoRA adapters and use multi-LoRA serving: one copy of the base model in GPU memory, adapters loaded or swapped per request, and kernels that batch requests for different adapters together (as vLLM and others support). This avoids 50 full model copies. Group heavy-traffic adapters on dedicated replicas and keep a cache of hot adapters on the GPU.

q: How do you choose between a hosted API and self-hosting an open model?
a: Hosted APIs give top quality, no infrastructure work, elastic scale and fast iteration, priced per token. Self-hosting gives control over data residency, latency and customization, and can be cheaper at high, steady volume, but needs GPU capacity planning, serving expertise, monitoring and upgrades. Decide on quality for your task (measured on your eval set), data and compliance needs, volume and traffic shape, latency targets and team skills; many teams use both, routing by task.

q: Why does <abbr title="Time To First Token">TTFT</abbr> increase in <abbr title="Retrieval-Augmented Generation">RAG</abbr> and agent applications?
a: Before generation starts, the application may embed the query, search an index, rerank, call tools, and then send a much longer prompt, which lengthens prefill. Each step adds latency, and agent loops repeat it per step. Mitigations: parallelize retrieval steps, cache embeddings and results, trim context, use prefix caching for stable parts, stream partial results, and run cheap steps on small models.

q: Autoencoder vs <abbr title="Variational Autoencoder">VAE</abbr>: why can't a plain autoencoder generate good samples?
a: A plain autoencoder only learns to reconstruct training inputs; nothing constrains where codes land, so the latent space has gaps and irregular regions, and decoding a random point often produces nonsense. A VAE encodes each input as a distribution and adds a KL penalty pulling every encoding toward a standard normal, so the latent space is continuous and covered: sampling \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) and decoding gives plausible outputs.

q: Explain the two terms of the <abbr title="Variational Autoencoder">VAE</abbr> <abbr title="Evidence Lower Bound">ELBO</abbr>.
a: The reconstruction term \(\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x \mid z)]\) rewards decoding the input accurately from its sampled code. The KL term \(D_{KL}(q(z \mid x)\,\|\,p(z))\) penalizes encodings that stray from the prior, which regularizes the latent space and makes sampling possible. Maximizing their difference maximizes a lower bound on the data log-likelihood; their balance (scaled by β in β-VAE) trades sharpness against latent-space structure.

q: Why is the reparameterization trick needed?
a: The ELBO requires sampling \(z\) from \(q(z \mid x)\), and you can't backpropagate through a random sampling step. Writing \(z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon\) with \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) moves the randomness into an input that doesn't depend on the parameters, so \(z\) becomes a deterministic, differentiable function of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), and gradients reach the encoder.

q: Why are <abbr title="Variational Autoencoder">VAE</abbr> samples blurry?
a: With a Gaussian likelihood, the reconstruction term is effectively MSE, which is minimized by the average of all plausible outputs for a given code, and averages of sharp images are blurry. The KL term also limits how much information each code carries, so fine detail isn't encoded. Remedies: perceptual or adversarial losses (VAE-GAN), discrete latents (VQ-VAE), or using the VAE only as a compressor while another model (diffusion, autoregressive) models the latents.

q: Explain the <abbr title="Generative Adversarial Network">GAN</abbr> objective.
a: The discriminator maximizes \(\mathbb{E}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]\), learning to output high probability for real data and low for fakes; the generator minimizes the same expression, learning to produce samples the discriminator accepts. At the optimal discriminator, the generator is minimizing the Jensen–Shannon divergence between data and generated distributions. In practice the generator maximizes \(\log D(G(z))\) to avoid weak gradients early in training.

q: What is mode collapse, and how is it mitigated?
a: The generator finds a few outputs that fool the discriminator and produces only those, ignoring the rest of the data distribution: low diversity despite good-looking samples. Mitigations: Wasserstein loss with gradient penalty (smoother, more informative gradients), minibatch discrimination or feature statistics that let the discriminator detect lack of diversity, unrolled GAN training, spectral normalization, and multiple generators. Diffusion models largely avoid it by design.

q: Why did WGAN help?
a: The original objective relates to the Jensen–Shannon divergence, which saturates when real and generated distributions don't overlap, giving the generator vanishing gradients. WGAN minimizes an approximation of the Wasserstein (earth-mover) distance, which still changes smoothly when distributions are far apart, using a critic constrained to be 1-Lipschitz (by weight clipping, or better, a gradient penalty). Training is more stable and the critic's loss correlates with sample quality.

q: What does <abbr title="Fréchet Inception Distance">FID</abbr> measure?
a: Fréchet Inception Distance embeds real and generated images with an Inception network, fits a Gaussian (mean and covariance) to each set of features, and computes the Fréchet distance between the two Gaussians. Lower is better; it captures both quality and diversity. Caveats: it depends on the feature network, needs many samples, is biased with small sample sizes, and doesn't measure prompt alignment (use CLIP score or human preference for that).

q: Explain the forward and reverse processes in diffusion models.
a: The forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise according to a fixed schedule until the data becomes pure noise; thanks to Gaussian properties, \(x_t\) can be sampled directly from \(x_0\) as \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\epsilon\). The reverse process is learned: a network predicts the added noise (or the clean image, or a velocity) at each step, and sampling starts from noise and denoises step by step to generate new data.

q: What does the diffusion network predict, and what is the loss?
a: Commonly the noise \(\epsilon\) that was added to produce \(x_t\), trained with mean squared error between the true and predicted noise at a randomly sampled timestep. Predicting noise is equivalent to estimating the score (gradient of log density) up to scaling. Alternatives predict the clean image \(x_0\) or the velocity \(v\), which can be more stable at some noise levels; all are interconvertible.

q: What is classifier-free guidance?
a: Train one denoiser both with the condition (such as the text prompt) and without it, by randomly dropping the condition during training. At sampling time, compute both predictions and extrapolate: \(\hat\epsilon = \epsilon(x_t, \varnothing) + w(\epsilon(x_t, c) - \epsilon(x_t, \varnothing))\). Guidance scale \(w\) trades diversity for prompt adherence and image quality. It removed the need for a separate classifier and is standard in text-to-image models.

q: Why is diffusion sampling slow, and how is it sped up?
a: Each sample needs many sequential denoising steps (hundreds to a thousand originally), each a full network evaluation. Speed-ups: better samplers and ODE solvers (DDIM, DPM-Solver) needing 20–50 steps; latent diffusion so each step is cheaper; flow matching with straighter trajectories; and distillation (progressive, consistency, adversarial) to 1–4 steps. Smaller or quantized denoisers and caching also help.

q: Why diffuse in latent space?
a: Pixel space is enormous (a 1024×1024 RGB image has about 3 million values), and most of that detail is perceptually redundant. A VAE compresses images about 8× per side into a latent that keeps the semantic and perceptual content; running diffusion there cuts compute and memory dramatically, enabling high resolution on consumer GPUs, while the VAE decoder restores detail.

q: How does text conditioning work in Stable Diffusion?
a: A text encoder (CLIP's, and in newer models also T5) turns the prompt into a sequence of token embeddings. The denoiser attends to them through cross-attention layers: queries from image latent features, keys and values from the text embeddings, so each region of the image can draw on relevant words. Classifier-free guidance strengthens the effect at sampling time.

q: What is flow matching?
a: A way to train continuous-time generative models by regressing a neural velocity field onto a target velocity that transports noise to data along a chosen path, often a straight line between a noise sample and a data sample (rectified flow). Sampling integrates that velocity field from noise to data. Training is simple and stable, and straighter paths allow good samples with fewer integration steps; several recent image models use it.

q: How does a LLaVA-style model connect a vision encoder to an <abbr title="Large Language Model">LLM</abbr>?
a: A pretrained vision encoder (a CLIP or SigLIP ViT) turns the image into patch features; a small projector (linear layer or MLP) maps each feature into the LLM's embedding space; those vectors are inserted into the token sequence as image tokens alongside the text. Training first aligns the projector on image–caption pairs with the other parts frozen, then instruction-tunes on visual question answering and conversation data.

q: Early vs late fusion in multimodal models.
a: Late fusion encodes each modality with its own pretrained encoder and combines them later (projector or cross-attention into an LLM): cheaper, reuses strong unimodal models, modular. Early fusion tokenizes all modalities into one sequence and trains a single model on them jointly from the start: deeper cross-modal interaction and native generation in several modalities, but much more expensive and harder to train.

q: How would you build question answering over scanned PDFs?
a: Options: (1) OCR plus layout parsing into text and tables, then a normal RAG pipeline; (2) a vision-language model that reads page images directly (better for charts, forms and complex layouts); or (3) retrieval over page-image embeddings with a VLM answering from the top pages. Production often mixes them: extract text for search, render pages for the VLM, cite page numbers, and evaluate on real documents for extraction accuracy and faithfulness.

q: Explain the Bellman equation.
a: It expresses a value recursively: the value of a state (or state–action pair) equals the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state. For a policy, \(V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma V^\pi(s')]\). The optimality version, \(Q^*(s, a) = \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma \max_{a'}Q^*(s', a')]\), defines the best achievable values. Dynamic programming solves these equations with a known model; TD methods and Q-learning approximate them from samples.

q: On-policy vs off-policy learning.
a: On-policy methods learn the value or improve the policy that is generating the data (SARSA, REINFORCE, PPO): stable, but data from older policies must be discarded or corrected. Off-policy methods learn about a target policy (often the greedy one) from data generated by a different behavior policy (Q-learning, DQN with replay): more sample-efficient because old data can be reused, but can be less stable and needs corrections such as importance sampling for policy methods.

q: Monte Carlo vs temporal-difference learning.
a: Monte Carlo waits for the episode to end and uses the actual return as the target: unbiased but high variance, and it needs episodes to finish. TD updates after each step with a bootstrapped target \(r + \gamma V(s')\): biased because it relies on the current estimate, but much lower variance, works online and in continuing tasks. TD(λ) and n-step returns interpolate between them.

q: Why does <abbr title="Deep Q-Network">DQN</abbr> use experience replay and a target network?
a: Consecutive transitions are highly correlated and the data distribution shifts as the policy changes, which destabilizes neural network training; sampling random minibatches from a replay buffer breaks correlations and reuses data. And because the TD target uses the same network being updated, the target moves with every step and training can oscillate or diverge; a target network updated only periodically holds targets fixed for a while.

q: Derive the policy gradient.
a: \(J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim \pi_ heta}[R( au)] = \int p_ heta( au)R( au)\,d au\). Then \( abla J = \int abla p_ heta( au)R( au)\,d au = \int p_ heta( au) abla\log p_ heta( au)R( au)\,d au\) using \( abla p = p\, abla\log p\). The trajectory log-probability is the sum of log policy terms plus environment dynamics, which don't depend on \( heta\), so \( abla J = \mathbb{E}[\sum_t abla\log\pi_ heta(a_t \mid s_t)R( au)]\). Using the return from time \(t\) onward (causality) gives REINFORCE.

q: Why subtract a baseline in policy gradients?
a: Raw returns make gradient estimates very noisy: every action in a good episode gets pushed up, even bad ones. Subtracting a baseline that depends only on the state keeps the gradient unbiased, since \(\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi}[\nabla\log\pi(a \mid s)]\,b(s) = 0\), but greatly reduces variance. Using \(V(s)\) as the baseline means actions are reinforced according to their advantage, how much better than expected they turned out.

q: What does <abbr title="Proximal Policy Optimization">PPO</abbr>'s clipping do?
a: It limits how far one update can move the policy from the policy that collected the data. The probability ratio between new and old policies is clipped to \([1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon]\), and the objective takes the minimum of the clipped and unclipped terms, so there's no benefit in pushing an action's probability further once the ratio leaves that range. This approximates a trust region cheaply, prevents destructive updates, and allows several epochs of updates on each batch.

q: Explain exploration vs exploitation and compare ε-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling.
a: Exploitation picks the best-known option; exploration tries others to learn whether they're better. ε-greedy explores uniformly at random with probability ε: simple but wastes exploration on clearly bad arms. UCB adds an optimism bonus that shrinks as an arm is tried more, so it explores uncertain arms systematically. Thompson sampling samples from each arm's posterior and picks the best sample, exploring in proportion to the probability each arm is optimal; it often performs best in practice and handles delayed feedback well.

q: How is text generation framed as RL in <abbr title="Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback">RLHF</abbr>?
a: The LLM is the policy; the state is the prompt plus the tokens generated so far; each action is the next token; an episode is one complete response. A reward model scores the finished response, and a per-token KL penalty against the reference (SFT) model is subtracted so the policy doesn't drift into reward hacking or gibberish. PPO maximizes this reward using a value model as the critic for advantage estimates.

q: What is the credit assignment problem?
a: When a reward arrives only at the end (a game won, a response judged good), it's unclear which earlier actions deserve the credit. RL handles it with discounting, value functions that estimate future reward from intermediate states, advantage estimation (GAE), and, for LLMs, process rewards that score intermediate reasoning steps rather than only the final answer.

q: Walk through the stages of <abbr title="Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback">RLHF</abbr>.
a: (1) SFT: fine-tune the base model on demonstrations of good responses. (2) Reward model: for many prompts, sample several responses, have humans rank or compare them, and train a model to score responses with a pairwise Bradley–Terry loss. (3) RL: optimize the SFT policy with PPO to maximize the reward model's score minus a KL penalty against the SFT reference. Iterate with fresh preference data from the improved policy, and evaluate helpfulness and harmlessness throughout.

q: What is <abbr title="Supervised Fine-Tuning">SFT</abbr>, and why mask the prompt tokens?
a: Supervised fine-tuning trains a pretrained model on (instruction, response) pairs with next-token cross-entropy, teaching it to behave like an assistant. Loss is computed only on response tokens because the goal is to learn to produce good answers given prompts, not to model or imitate user messages; including prompt tokens wastes capacity and can teach the model to generate user turns. The chat template's role tokens make the boundary explicit.

q: Why does <abbr title="Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback">RLHF</abbr> need a <abbr title="Kullback–Leibler divergence">KL</abbr> penalty?
a: The reward model is a learned, imperfect proxy for human preferences, accurate only near the distribution it was trained on. Optimizing it hard pushes the policy toward outputs that exploit its errors (reward hacking) and away from fluent, diverse language. The KL penalty to the SFT reference keeps the policy close to known-good behavior, limiting over-optimization; β sets the trade-off between reward and staying close.

q: What is reward hacking? Give an example.
a: The policy finds ways to get high reward that don't reflect what we actually want, by exploiting flaws in the reward signal. Examples: responses growing much longer because the reward model prefers length; excessive hedging or flattery; confident-sounding wrong answers that look authoritative; in code, special-casing tests instead of fixing the bug. Mitigations: KL regularization, better and refreshed reward models, ensembles, length control, verifiable rewards where possible, and evaluation by humans.

q: Why is <abbr title="Proximal Policy Optimization">PPO</abbr>-based <abbr title="Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback">RLHF</abbr> memory-hungry?
a: It keeps four large networks: the policy being trained (with gradients and optimizer state), a frozen reference model for the KL term, the reward model, and a value model (critic) that's usually as large as the policy, also trained. It also generates samples during training, which needs inference machinery and KV caches. That's why DPO (two models, no sampling) and GRPO (no critic) became popular.

q: Explain the intuition behind <abbr title="Direct Preference Optimization">DPO</abbr>'s loss.
a: DPO uses the fact that the optimal KL-regularized policy implies a reward equal to \(\beta\) times the log-ratio of policy to reference probabilities. Plugging that implicit reward into the Bradley–Terry preference loss gives a classification-style objective: increase \(\log\pi_\theta(y_w)/\pi_{ref}(y_w)\) relative to \(\log\pi_\theta(y_l)/\pi_{ref}(y_l)\). Gradients are weighted by how wrong the model currently is about each pair. No reward model, no sampling, no critic.

q: <abbr title="Direct Preference Optimization">DPO</abbr> vs <abbr title="Proximal Policy Optimization">PPO</abbr>: trade-offs.
a: DPO is simpler (supervised-style training), cheaper (policy plus frozen reference), more stable, and needs no reward model. PPO is on-policy: it learns from its own fresh samples, can exploit a reward model or verifier that generalizes beyond the preference dataset, and handles non-preference rewards such as unit tests. DPO can over-fit its fixed dataset and push probability toward unlikely outputs; iterative or online DPO narrows the gap. Choose DPO for preference alignment with a good dataset, RL for verifiable rewards and frontier tuning.

q: Why keep a reference model in <abbr title="Direct Preference Optimization">DPO</abbr>?
a: The loss is defined in terms of log-probability ratios between the policy and the reference, which is what the implicit KL regularization becomes. Without the reference, the model could raise the chosen response's probability by degenerate means and drift far from fluent behavior. Variants like ORPO and SimPO remove it by changing the objective, adding an SFT term or length normalization to keep training anchored.

q: What is Constitutional AI?
a: A method for training harmless, helpful assistants with AI feedback guided by a written set of principles. In the supervised stage the model critiques and revises its own responses according to the principles, and is fine-tuned on the revisions. In the RL stage, the model judges pairs of responses by the principles, and those AI-generated preferences train a reward model used for RL (RLAIF). It scales oversight, makes values explicit, and aims for models that explain their objections rather than refusing evasively.

q: <abbr title="Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback">RLHF</abbr> vs <abbr title="Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback">RLAIF</abbr>.
a: Both train a reward model from preference comparisons and then do RL. In RLHF, people make the comparisons: high-quality signal of real preferences, but slow, expensive, inconsistent, and limited in volume. In RLAIF, an AI model makes them, usually guided by principles or rubrics: cheap and scalable, and consistent, but bounded by the judge's own abilities and biases. Many pipelines combine them, using people for calibration and difficult or high-stakes cases.

q: What are the risks of using an <abbr title="Large Language Model">LLM</abbr> as a judge or reward model?
a: Biases (favoring longer answers, its own style or its own outputs, the first position in a comparison), blind spots shared with the policy, and susceptibility to manipulation (outputs that flatter or address the judge). Optimizing hard against it invites reward hacking. Mitigate by calibrating against human labels, randomizing order, using rubrics and multiple judges, mixing in human and verifiable signals, and auditing high-reward outputs.

q: What is sycophancy, and where does it come from?
a: A model telling users what they want to hear: agreeing with incorrect claims, changing a correct answer when challenged, or praising weak work. It emerges partly from preference training, because people tend to rate agreeable, validating answers higher. Mitigations include preference data that rewards respectful disagreement and honesty, principles that prioritize truthfulness, evaluations that test consistency under pushback, and system prompts that ask for candor.

q: Quality vs quantity in <abbr title="Supervised Fine-Tuning">SFT</abbr> data: what matters more?
a: Quality and diversity. Experiments like LIMA showed a few thousand carefully curated, varied, high-quality examples can produce strong instruction following, because pretraining already supplies most knowledge and SFT mainly teaches format and behavior. Low-quality or inconsistent data teaches bad habits, and data that answers beyond the model's knowledge encourages hallucination. Deduplicate, filter, balance task types, and evaluate rather than scale blindly.

q: How do you evaluate whether alignment training worked?
a: Measure several things at once: helpfulness (win rates against a baseline judged by people or calibrated LLM judges, task benchmarks), harmlessness (red-team prompts, refusal rates on harmful requests), over-refusal on benign but sensitive-sounding prompts, honesty (calibration, sycophancy tests, hallucination rates), and capability regressions on standard benchmarks. Check for length bias in judge-based evaluations and test on held-out, recent prompts.

q: Why does chain-of-thought prompting improve accuracy?
a: Each generated token gets a fixed amount of computation, so a model answering immediately must solve the whole problem in one step. Writing intermediate steps spends more computation, lets later steps attend to earlier results like a scratchpad, and breaks the problem into pieces that look like patterns from training. The gains are large mainly for big models; small models often produce plausible but wrong reasoning.

q: What is self-consistency?
a: Sample several chain-of-thought solutions at non-zero temperature, extract each final answer, and return the most common one. Different reasoning paths make different mistakes, so the majority answer is more reliable than a single greedy one. It costs N times the tokens and needs answers that can be compared (numbers, options, short strings). Weighted voting with a verifier is a stronger variant.

q: Process reward models vs outcome reward models.
a: An ORM scores only the final answer (or the whole response); its labels are cheap and can be exact (tests, answer match), but it gives coarse credit and can reward lucky answers reached by flawed reasoning. A PRM scores each step, giving fine-grained credit, catching errors early, and enabling step-level search, but step labels are expensive and PRMs can be exploited too. ORMs suit RL with verifiable rewards; PRMs suit verification and search at inference.

q: What are verifiable rewards, and why do they matter for RL?
a: Rewards computed by a program rather than a learned model: checking a math answer against the reference, running unit tests, validating a proof or a format. They're accurate, cheap, consistent and much harder to hack than a learned reward model, which makes it possible to run long RL training that steadily improves reasoning. The limitation is coverage: many valuable tasks have no exact checker.

q: What is <abbr title="Group Relative Policy Optimization">GRPO</abbr> and how does it differ from <abbr title="Proximal Policy Optimization">PPO</abbr>?
a: GRPO samples a group of responses per prompt, scores them, and uses each response's reward normalized by the group's mean and standard deviation as its advantage, applied to all its tokens. It then uses PPO's clipped surrogate with a KL penalty to a reference model. Unlike PPO, it has no learned value model (critic), saving memory and removing a source of instability; the group itself provides the baseline. It's well-suited to sparse, pass/fail rewards.

q: What did DeepSeek-R1 show?
a: That large-scale RL with simple verifiable rewards can teach a model to reason with long chains of thought, self-verification and backtracking; R1-Zero did it from a base model without SFT, though with readability problems. R1's full pipeline combined a small cold-start SFT set, RL, rejection-sampled SFT and a final RL stage. It also showed reasoning traces from a large model can be distilled into small open models effectively, and it did all this with openly released weights and a detailed report.

q: What is test-time compute scaling?
a: Improving answers by spending more computation at inference rather than training a larger model: generating longer reasoning, sampling many candidates and selecting with a verifier or vote, or searching over reasoning steps.
